Horton Plains National Park is unlike anywhere else I visited in Sri Lanka — high-altitude grasslands, cloud forests, waterfalls, and epic cliffside views all wrapped into one peaceful hike. If you're looking for a break from the heat and beaches, this is a fantastic escape into cool, fresh mountain air. We started the 9.5 km loop trail just after sunrise. The park opens at 6:00 AM, and I highly recommend getting there early. Not only do you beat the crowds, but you also have a better chance of catching clear skies before the mist rolls in over World’s End  the highlight of the hike. The trail is mostly flat with a few rocky or muddy sections. It takes about 2.5 to 3 hours depending on your pace and how often you stop to admire the scenery. Along the way, you’ll pass through rolling plains, dense forest, and misty stretches that feel almost otherworldly. Wildlife is shy but present we saw sambars (large deer), plenty of birds, and lots of interesting plants. When you reach World’s End, the view is jaw-dropping  a sheer cliff dropping almost 800 meters, with tea estates and distant hills stretching into the horizon. Mini World’s End comes a bit earlier on the trail and offers a similar, though less dramatic, viewpoint. After that, Baker’s Falls is a lovely place to stop, rest, and enjoy the sound of rushing water. Horton Plains isn’t about adrenaline  it’s about quiet, natural beauty. It’s not crowded (especially early), and the air is cool and refreshing. You feel totally immersed in nature.

On clear mornings, you can even see the southern coastline from above the clouds! ☁️🌊 🌸 With rare flora, crystal-clear streams, and graceful sambar deer roaming freely, Horton Plains is a paradise for nature lovers, hikers, and photographers alike. 🦌📸 Whether it’s the refreshing trek through scenic trails, the magical sunrise, or the silence of the mist-covered mountains – Horton Plains is truly a place where nature speaks to your soul. 💚

Along the way, I spotted elusive wildlife, from colorful birds to curious sambar deer, making each turn a small adventure. Horton Plains isn’t just a hike; it’s a journey into the heart of Sri Lanka’s serene highlands.

Horton Plains is a breathtaking gem in Sri Lanka, offering misty landscapes, rolling grasslands, and rich biodiversity. The highlight is World’s End, a dramatic cliff with stunning views, especially at sunrise. The trek is moderate, surrounded by cloud forests, wildflowers, and occasional sambar deer. Baker’s Falls adds to the charm with its refreshing beauty. The cool climate makes it ideal for hiking, but mornings are best before the mist sets in. A must-visit for nature lovers, hikers, and photographers seeking serene beauty. Horton Plains truly captures the untouched essence of Sri Lanka’s highlands.

We visited Horton Plains, and it was truly one of the highlights of my trip to Sri Lanka. We started the trek early in the morning around 6:30 AM, which I highly recommend to avoid the mist at World’s End. The trail is well-marked and not too difficult, perfect for moderate-level hikers. The views from World’s End and Mini World’s End were absolutely stunning, especially before the clouds rolled in. Bakers Falls was also beautiful and worth the small detour. We spotted some sambar deer along the way, and the landscape is incredibly unique, a mix of grassland and cloud forest that you don’t see often. The weather was cool and refreshing, which made the walk even more enjoyable. Do bring water, a light jacket, and good walking shoes. Also, no plastic bags are allowed inside the park, which is great for conservation. Highly recommended for nature lovers, photographers, and anyone looking to escape into peaceful surroundings.

Beautiful nature greenery!  Weather was amazing in April when I visited. Had a tour guide for my walk there. Started to walk at 7.30am.  Mist and cool weather helped to keep me energised. For my speed, I took 4 hours to complete the walk. 'World's End' summit was beautiful! at that height! Rocks along the way looked colourful. Intermittent ups and downs.  We took the route that was more downwards walking instead of the opposite direction which was very well planned!

We had a very early start in a tuk tuk from Nuwara Eliya at  5am!  Our driver was amazing and put the sides down as it was really cold.  We stopped to watch the sunrise which was lovely and continued to the park.  He has seen leopards here but not on the paths to worlds end.  There is a toilet opposite the ticket counter, then you walk a bit to the museum and the entry just after that where they check for plastic.  They will remove stickers or labels off bottles.  We were fine and did the walk  clockwise, it was nice and relatively easy.  Wear good walking shoes and our accommodation had supplied us a packed breakfast which was really nice of them.  We sat and ate that at worlds end and got a lovely view.  It seemed a popular spot to sit and have breakfast.  There was only 6 people there (3 of us) which was really peaceful. The clouds come in pretty quick.  We enjoyed bakers falls and walked back.  You strip off your layers as you go along as it does get quite warm fast. As we were leaving a lot of people were arriving, the view was long gone but it is still a nice walk.  The alpine grasses remind me of New Zealand. It is expensive to enter, I enjoyed it but wouldn't do it again, would rather do another trek with a guide here.

This is a great place for all outdoor explorers. There are a few trekking paths, and the views are spectacular. I recommend starting your journey in the morning. You will need to purchase a ticket, but it’s not very expensive. Along the way, you can see a few waterfalls depending on the route you take. The shortest route takes about 2 hours to complete, but you can turn back at any point if you feel tired. Make sure to bring water and some snacks. Note that polythene is not allowed, so use paper bags instead. You can drive to the starting point, where you’ll find parking, and from there, you’ll need to walk. There are a few shops for snacks and clean washrooms at the starting point. Overall, this is a must-visit place if you are in Sri Lanka, and it’s not a very challenging hike. I’ve been there twice and would definitely go again. On the way, you’ll also pass a few farms, which you can visit if you’re interested.

All the family enjoyed this hike which varies from easy on a level path to moderately difficult on the ascent/descent on clay type soil and rocky, uneven paths. Following rain the previous day, the paths were a little muddy and slippery in parts. In August, it was not too busy and we had plenty of time to go at our own pace and see the sights which included Baker’s Falls, Mini Worlds End and Worlds End. We reached Worlds End at 8am but mist had already descended which obscured the view. We got to tick off some more wildlife - wild boar, Sambar deer, Rhino-horned lizards and  chameleons. There were many beautiful flowers to see en route. A local guide was extremely helpful and gave us lots of good information along the way. There was a small visitor’s centre worth visiting briefly.

It is a nice location, with good views. However, tourists should not waste your money here, as you will pay 150 times the local price. Took about 4hrs for a 9.5km trail. Please note that this is not a trail for casual walkers, or the young or elderly. There is no such warning or information about the conditions of the trail when you are buying the entry tickets. Wide open views for only about 25% of the hike, because 75% of the trail is within hilly forested areas. And about 90% of the trail is on uneven ground. My Garmin fitness tracker recorded that we estimatedly climbed 42 flights of stairs uphill, and 51 flights of stairs downhill. While it is a beautiful place for a challenging hike, my poor review is because of the entry fees. Foreigners are charged around 40usd, which is about an exorbitant 150 times more than a local ticket. The 25usd price is misleading, because you also need to pay government taxes and service charges. There wasn't any indication of any services provided, or why we were charged for it. Toilets did not have much privacy. The road leading to the park was badly maintained, and full of  pot holes. Man made trails were horrible and poorly maintained.

Honestly we had seen mixed reviews but are so glad we went and did the trail. Yes there is a pretty hefty cost, but it is a UNESCO site and you do get to walk through multiple environments. The trail is pretty easy to moderate - big tip - when you get to the start point there are two ways to go - go to the right, way less stairs and much better walk.

The park is new and obviously designed to make it easy for many people to see this part of Sri Lanka.  There are a few things to know ahead of time.  They are very serious about possible trash, so no containers of yogurt (as an example) are allowed in.  They prefer reusable water bottles, but turned a blind eye (since we had no idea) though they did use a knife to remove all the labels from our hotel-provided plastic bottles).  The trails themselves are wide and extremely well-groomed.  Following the trails is easy (except at a very few crossroads).  The system of marking the trails is not really complete yet.  But the views are stunning - both the vistas, the overlook in the chasm called 'end of the world', and the close-ups while hiking in the forests.

Visiting Horton Plains in Sri Lanka offers a unique experience where the lush greenery and serene landscapes remind one of the Scottish Highlands or the Irish countryside. The highlight of the area is the 'World's End' - a spectacular viewpoint with breathtaking vistas. However, travelers should note that reaching this spot is quite a challenge. The path to World's End is not just a leisurely stroll; it involves navigating steep, uneven terrain with multiple climbs. It's essential to wear comfortable, sturdy shoes to tackle these paths. This trek might not be suitable for those with physical limitations, knee injuries, or families traveling with small children due to its demanding nature. Moreover, it's crucial to consider the weather before planning your visit. The rainy season can be particularly hazardous in this region, with risks of sudden floods. Therefore, it’s best to avoid monsoon periods for a safer and more enjoyable experience. In summary, Horton Plains offers a stunning natural escape for the active and adventurous traveler, but it requires good preparation and a consideration of physical abilities. It's a place that leaves you in awe of nature's beauty, but also reminds you of its demands

Went to Horton place this morning. At 5 o'clock in the tuk tuk to drive an hour from Nuwara Eliya. We got there at 6am. There was already quite a line of drivers in front of the cash register, which opens at 6 am. The entrance fee was even more expensive than the $25. We had to pay 3290 rupees for the 3 of us and you also pay for the driver who can then drive to the starting point. That's another 5 km. We came across a group of deer. No further animals were seen in the area. I thought it was an exciting idea that the leopard is also walking around there. Apparently it doesn't attack humans ;-) At the starting point your bag will be opened and you will have to take out everything that is in the plastic. They offer paper bags. They take the labels off your water bottles. They were allowed inside. You can walk left and right. We went left and walked the more difficult route when you could choose. We didn't realize that at first and we wondered how all the 'oldies' were going to do this. You walk through very narrow, densely overgrown paths with an abyss next to you. Encountered 2 x toilets. Everything looks neat. It is quite a tough walk (9 km) with climbing and descending. Our legs were quite sore (also because we had only slept a few hours). It took us 3 hours. It is a completely different landscape than what you see elsewhere in the area.

My friend and I visited in January 2023. Overall, I would recommend choosing antoher of the many attractions in the hill country over Horton Plains. Why go: it's a pretty and clean walk through a high-altitute plateau to a wide outlook down to the plains. We saw some deer in the open fields and interesting descriptions of the cloud forest. The walk is comparable in enjoyment to many temperate walks elsewhere. Easy to hire a return car trip from Nuwara Eliya (10,000 LKR). You can easily do the circular walk in 2-3hrw. Take sturdy shoes and a warm top layer. Start early: be at the park centre for 6:30am to get the best chance of the views before the clouds come in. If money is no question, then you will enjoy the park. Why skip: regretfully the park management seem to have taken to an extortion racket. A single person ticket for a foreigner will cost you around USD40 with the ticket price and the 'service charge', and even more if you actually want to pay in dollars (the clerk at the entrance will happily exchange to rupees for a hefty fee). That's probably about 40 times the price for locals. That is absurdly expensive for Sri Lankan standards and it's very expensive for what you get by Western standards, as it is just an unguided walk through the nature.

Get ready for a walk, walk and walk for approximately 9.4 kms !! (Pheww) Undoubtedly this hike will give you a beautiful experience of walking in sweat, clouds, mist, rain and breeze ! In the rains the rocks, the waking passage can be slippery making your hike really challenging. Till you reach bakers fall you will get an insight of your journey anyways !! One should be with very good quality hiking shoes with good grip which will be helpful while waking. Rain Coats, cap and some food stuffs are very important along with you. Remember to carry them in a paper bag as no plastics are allowed inside. We started our hike through Horton Plains early in the morning to catch a sunrise over the misty hills and terrains. What can I say, it was definitely worth waking up so early. We saw plenty of deers eating fresh grass even before we entered the main gate of the park, and then had an enjoyable walk along the route towards Baker's Falls. There are two options: you can start with the Falls and finish by the Little World's End or vice versa. We chose the first option and did not regret it. After we saw the sunrise, the sun quickly disappeared behind the clouds and we did not see it much until we reached the falls and the skies became blue. We took wonderful photos and had our packed breakfast right there on a bench, which was so romantic and enjoyable. When we continued our route towards the World's End, we realized how right we were in taking that path - we almost always hiked down rather than climbing up and it made our trekking way more comfortable and less tiring. The day before we hiked the Adam's Peak, so we could not feel our legs and feet after that and this path we chose turned out to be helpful :) Unfortunately, when we reached the World's End, a big cloud hung on top and covered all the view. We waited for 30 minutes and the situation remained the same. We still were pleased with the hike and the World's End because there was a certain mystery in this endless mist over the edge. You can literally feel you are on the edge of nowhere. P.S. In my opinion, you won't need a guide to hike Horton Plains. It is super easy and it is impossible to get lost on the way. There is literally only one path and it is a round journey, so whatever way you choose - you will end up in the same place. Only if a lady is solo and scared of being attacked or something??? But generally, for me it seemed peaceful and safe. And if a leopard comes out from a bush, I don't think that having a guide will be helpful right??))) Also the time you will spend there will be at least 4-5 hrs if you do not want to run along the whole route and wish to take nice pictures and just enjoy the nature around you. So don't listen to people who tell it is like a 3-hour hike. Maybe, if you don't complete the whole circle..)

This is a lovely trekking place with fresh air and beautiful scenery along the trekking paths. Some beautiful stops worth to check out are: 1. Little World’s End view point 2. Great World’s End view point 3. Baker’s Waterfalls We were so lucky to be able to see a wild Sambar Deer right in front of us up close before the starting point of the trek. Entrance fee is quite steep at LKR3,850 per person. Suggest to go early in the morning as we departed from our hotel at Nuwara Eliya at 5am. On the way up to Horton Plains, before reaching the ticket booth, we stopped at the roadside to watch the sunrise above the sea clouds. Horton Plains is a UNESCO World Heritage Site where is protected areas for its nature beauty. It is a plateau at 2100-2300 meters above sea level. Hence, be prepared for the warm clothing since it can be very chilly early in the morning. A complete route of hiking require at least half day time (4-5 hours depends on individual fitness level) and the trekking path is relatively easy for all age, but good walking shoes are necessary, plus adequate drinking water. Packing breakfast is advisable for people who do morning trek. Tight security check of the bag/ haversack at the entrance of trekking and no plastics allowed at the park. We were so glad that we did morning trek as the weather was cool and pleasant and completed our trek slightly before noon. Hence, most people do morning trek and be there early as there will be long queue for security check. An afternoon trekking would be warm and sweaty due to warmer weather in the day. We simply love this place and the beauty of Mother Nature!!!

We were on a small group tour and the walk to World's End and Baker's Fall has been one of the highlights of our trip so far. Quite rightly they don't allow any plastic containers in the park (other than water bottles with labels removed), so be prepared for a thorough bag check on arrival. Hortan plains is a plateau set on high mountains of Sri Lanka. It sits at a height of more than 2000 meters above sea level. This plateau spreads over 3150 hectares, and is a great attraction to both local and foreign tourists. It can be reached by motorable road from Pattipola or Ohiya. When you climb from below you can see how vegetation differs and weather becomes colder. When you enter the plateau you see it’s covered with mist and stunted trees due to the strong winds on the plains. Also you can find small ponds of water with water lilies. As you go further the trees become fewer but instead there are low growing bushes and more of a moor type of vegetation. Main attraction in Hortan plains is ‘Worlds End, a 700 meter breathtaking sheer drop. This drop has the most magnificent view of the sourthern wall of central highlands. Another attraction is Baker’s falls. It can be reached after a long walk through the forest. The plains are home for leopards,elk, monkeys and jackals. Plain is also home for many endemic plants. When you make a visit please make sure you do not harm the plants and animals and you will only observe the beauty of it. Worth making a trip.

It starts about 400 meters from the Entrance Gate. Start off early and aim to get there before 6.30am for the best views over World's End, before the mist & cloud cover the area. Take the route that goes to mini World's End first from left. The hike takes about 3 to 4 hours, do not forget to bring water, snack, umbrella (in case if it rains) and wear proper hiking shoes. You will first reach to Mini World's End ( 2 Kms from Entrance). From Mini worlds Ends to Greater World's End is further 3 Kms. Further to reach Baker's Falls you need to Walk 2 Kms. On the way you will get a Public Toilet which is not very clean & hygienic with no water tap in it. Returning back to gate you will get to see Chimney Pool (1.5 Kms from Greater World's End. There is only one toilet in entire route inside the Park, so try to use one before you leave your hotel, or else at the entrance of the national park, there is a toilet. Ticket price is well worth it. Grassland plains, mangrove forests. There is a restaurant outside the gate were you can refresh yourself . We paid LKR 7,950.00 for 2 person incl all. for the entrance ticket.

This national park is the source for four of Sri Lanka's major rivers, so it's not unusual to experience a bit of rain. Fortunately, the heavy rain dropped the night before our 9.5 km trek through the park, which took in the spectacular World's End. It made some uneven parts of the trail a bit slippery, so solid hiking shoes or, at minimum runners, are essential. Only a moderate level of fitness is required to navigate the main trail, which takes in World's End and Bakers Falls. However, anyone with some walking or climbing disability should take note that there are those uneven areas to negotiate. World's End is so called because of its 900 metre vertical cliff face that drops into the forest of the valley wall. It's hard to capture its scale in photographs. There are two viewing decks at World's End. Beware, particularly for children, that there are few barriers to prevent falls over the cliffs, both on the decks and on the short trail between decks. My impression was that the coiled razor wire would merely lacerate you during the fall rather than prevent it. The higher deck gives a much better view of the main cliff face. The steps down to Bakers Falls are also quite steep. Hortons Plains features a wide variety of landscape and an explosion of different colours from the many plant species that adorn the plain. The area is also a good place to see Sambar Deer, one of Sri Lanka's larger deer species.

The hike isn't too difficult, it's about 8 miles with a few portions of steeper climbing, but getting there in the morning allows you to see some GORGEOUS views. My driver gave me the tip of sitting and waiting at World's End because a lot can change in the scenery in a matter of minutes, and it was the best advice. I ate snacks I packed (remember to do this) and took a 40 minute rest up there and watched in awe as clouds and fog came in and out (at one point completely blocking the view and then clearing up to reveal a gorgeous drop and the plains beyond). I wanted to take pictures every time I turned the corner because I was treated to new views every mile or so - the diversity in ecosystems and flora/fauna is INSANE. If you're in Nuwara Eliya, make sure you make time for this hike! I actually stopped in Nuwara Eliya JUST so I could get out here! Definitely get an early start (apparently sometimes in the morning you can see deer and elephants if it's early enough!) so you're hiking when it's cooler and to beat the crowds.

We had a very unfortunate experience when buying tickets to enter Horton Plains National Park. We visited on the morning of Friday 12th July. Apologies for the long and less than positive review, I am also posting this hoping someone may be able to point me towards a way to lodge a complaint with the Park itself as I haven’t been able to find this online. Ticket prices are not advertised as prices tend to fluctuate so there is no price list at the ticket booth. We asked for “3 tickets, one person is local”, however this was interpreted as 3 tickets plus one local. A foreigner ticket at the time was ~2,650 rupees. With no price list, visitors the transaction is based purely on verbal communication with no calculator or screen to show how prices are calculated (there are three taxes on top of the ticket price). Understandably this is also a quick, rushed process during busy times such as when we visited. Unfortunately, we were unable to realise we were overcharged until we had driven 10 minutes from the ticket office to the park entrance. At the park entrance we spoke with a number of staff and based on what they advised we decided to enter the park rather than drive back and seek a refund (lucky we did this because as we found out, we would not have been refunded anyway and it would have ruined our visit). On our way out we approached the ticket booth and fortunately the same cashier was working (a middle aged man, moustache, larger, has worked at the park for over 15 years). We were very careful to politely inform that we were accidentally overcharged (e.g. we avoided saying “you overcharged us”, instead saying “we were accidentally overcharged”) however he immediately went on the defensive, became very rude and irrational and refused to help us. He accused us of being irresponsible and not communicating with him properly. He also said there is no possibility of a refund once a sale has been made and its the customers responsibility to know what they are being charged and that he does not make mistakes so it must be our fault. When we tried to explain that we were not trying to pass blame and a simple misunderstanding had occurred, he became argumentative and started insulting our tour guide/driver in Sinhalese and saying he was not looking after us properly. He refused to call the park manager (he said there was no phone reception, although all three of us had reception) and said nobody would help us because it was our fault. There was lots of back and forth about ticket prices not being advertised, no way of knowing what we have been charged for until transaction has been finalised etc. until we finally decided that nothing we did or said would help us obtain a refund. Overall, this left a very sour taste in our mouths and our tour guide/driver felt ashamed that a park ranger would behave in this way. Unfortunately, the cashier did not have an ounce of empathy and his behaviour screamed dishonesty and not a care on the world for doing what is right. Had he at least even tried to help us in the slightest, our experience with him would have been completely difference. Lesson: when buying tickets and you have a local guide to accompany you, be very clear to say X foreigner tickets and Y local ticket. Avoid assuming any statements like “3 people, one is local” as this will be interpreted as 3 foreigners, one local”. As for the park itself, it is beautiful and the views are amazing. It was lovely walking through such stunning scenery. However, the price is quite high especially in comparison to similar yet free experiences we have had in Sri Lanka as well as other national parks we have visited around the world.

The tuk tuk ride from Nuwara Eliya was 3500Rs. There was a long line for the toilets at the entrance but there are more toilets inside the park where the walk starts from. It’s quite a long drive from the park entrance to start of the walk, I had assumed the walk would start at the entrance but we saw no one walking along the road. We saw several Sambar Deer though! There are bag checks at the start of the walk where plastic is confiscated. Plastic drink bottles had the plastic labels torn off them. The walk clockwise to World’s End is pleasant with grasslands and bush. There are toilets near little worlds end. It was misty at World’s End but the mist came and went so we were still able to see out to some lakes south at times. It’s a neat spot for watching clouds of mist rise over the 800m drop. Start early morning, ideally at 7-8am, there might be some mist later (and too hot). Foreigners pay ca 2800 LKR, locals 60 LKR. Definitely don’t miss this trip, it was probably our best experience in Sri Lanka.

In summary, this is a nice walk, but rather expensive if you compare it to walking in other national parks.

It's not the greatest walk I've been on, but it was different and enjoyable.  I wouldn't want to do it in the middle of the day as I thought it was quite hot when we walked - from about 7.20 to 10.30. There is a cloud forest in this area so you'd have to get there very early or be very lucky to strike the World's End without a lot of cloud.  But they said, I didn't mind standing near the edge and watching the cloud roll in and up and over the cliff face.  Sit long enough and the cloud lightens enough for you to see the valley below and some of the tea fields. If you follow the track on the left it is the shortest to the viewing platforms but it makes the walk back via the falls a steeper climb, so I personally preferred walking anti-clockwise and getting to the platform after the crowds and then having an easier walk back along the less steep ridge. Frogs, forest pigeon and a Sri Lankan giant squirrel were our rewards for walking this trail.  The squirrel looked like an Australian tree kangaroo in the face but had a large bushy tail.  You can hear the bear monkeys in the jungle here as well and we're so lucky in that on the very bumpy drive back down the plateau a bear monkey was posing for us on a tree Top. So keep a look out. As walks go it was moderate - some steep slippery sections, and the landscape it crosses was quite interesting - undulating hills, interspersed with grasslands and forests. I don't know what the park fees were as we did it as part of a package so in some respects it's better not to know and as I think the most expensive fees, it was nice to see the Rangers being very vigilant with hikers as far as long plastics go and to search each bag and advise to bring everything back out. So surprisingly I saw very little plastic litter - the off pieces carelessly dropped but good to see they are trying to keep the area litter free - except the toilet area - unfortunately full of rubbish.

This is a fair distance from Nuwara Eliya and at least from our hotel it would appear impossible to get there for sunrise unless you were prepared to get up very early. Although it is only 4.5kms to World’s End the walking at times is not easy and I can’t imagine doing it in the dark. It is going to take you between 2.5 and 3 hours of walking. The weather in this part of the world is very unpredictable and I think you should see whether you can cancel your trip if the weather is not good. We were lucky and had a very clear day. Although you go for the spectacular views, don’t rush and try to just enjoy the peace and quiet. From our experience, walk anti-clockwise as there is otherwise a very steep and difficult climb near Baker’s Falls.

Though popularly known as Hortan Plains, the locations' original name is Maha Eliya Plains (මහ එළිය තැන්න / Great Open Plains) which is unknown even for many locals. It was renamed during  British era after Sir Robert Wilmot-Horton. There is an unproved facts that he was one of the famous elephant hunter in the area when British ruled the country. One of the iconic identity of the country  located  about 32 km from Nuwaraeliya in central  highlands. This UNESCO world heritage site is a live proof of rich  biodiversity of Sri Lanka with a massive collection of endemic flora and fauna. Specialty is, some are endemic to Greta Open plains. It provides headwaters for main three rivers Mahaweli, Kelani and Walawe. Though climate is cold, covering the entire area is tiring. Make sure not to take plastic and dump garbage. Importantly, damaging flora and fauna or taking samples are strictly prohibited. Selfies caused number of deaths in reason past so better be cautious. If you slip, you will end up reaching Balangoda in Sabaragamuwa province low lands; BUT WON'T BE ALIVE.

Only 26 km from Nuwara Eliya but a long, steep and winding drive up to the plains. Mist rolls in later in the morning and often the views are obscured. It's a 5 km hike to World's End and back via Baker's Falls, also worth seeing. Visited Horton Plains and hiked two different trails for a total of 12 kilometers. Scenes are spectacular: you’ll pass so many beautiful vistas and scenic overlooks that you’ll run out of smartphone battery power before running out of photos to take. This is a must do trek but arrive early at the park (0800 latest).  There are many trying to get in and the lines to get tickets are quite long.

Facts: Circular walk is 11.6 KM, altitude is 2100-2300 M (it 7000+ feet), so oxygen is less at this height (down from 20.9% effective to circa. 15.5%) . If a hot day then this walk is strenuous but very doable (take plenty water). Half way round is Worlds End a vertical and panoramic viewpoint which is something (careful here a tourist lost their life “selfie” taking recently). Disappointment for me was the lack of wildlife - I had expected a richly biodiverse assortment of mammals and birds and encountered very little.

This is a national park and it does require money but I have to wonder where it goes. We were told 3 different distances to the various 'signature spots' and the signposts give a fourth opinion. This should not be attempted by anyone with a hip, knee or ankle problem and hiking boots are almost a necessity. The tracks are not maintained in any way and consist of reasonably steep climbs and descents through deep ruts strewn with boulders, rocks and loose stones. Furthermore it is suppoesed to be a nature walk, and we started before sunrise, only to find around 100 vehicles at the the first gate with several 100 tourists clamouring for tickets. We entered and drove 5kms to the second gate to find even more vehicles and people. Goodness knows what this is like later in the day although when we left at about 9.30 am there must hjave been thousands in the park. As described, walking is difficult and the experience was not helped by crowds of mainly Asian tourists squawking incessantly and noisily with some even playing their radios for all to hear. The result - no wildlife. When we got to either of the World's Ends we could hardly see a not that impressive view for the crowds of photo and selfie taking tourists. There seemed to be neither control nor wardens on hand and most of the guides were more intent on chatting up their attractive customers than controlling the mobs. Our guide, who was embaraseed by the appalling behavious of the tourists and their mentors, did attempt to quieten the mobs but his efforts were in vain. He did advise us not to attempt a visit to Bakers Falls as that requires climbing and descending by holding on to mangrove roots as the tracks are in an even bigger mess. It is a not that impressive, expensive money spinner but for whom?

The walk starts early at 7am and was frosty, but warmed up. So wear layers first thing in the morning and have a rucksack to put things in as you warm up. Just a quick note on cost for those planning on doing the world's end walk (mainly because we hadn't appreciated it before going). The entry to the park is around 8400 rupees for two tourists, which is compared with the local's entry fee of 300-500 rupees. On top of the entry fee you also have your tuk-tuk/taxi fee. We paid a flat rate of 3500 rupees from Nuwara Eliya, which is apparently pretty standard. You can obviously split the cost by going in a big group, but I think you then pay extra on your ticket price for taking a larger vehicle. Obviously the cost goes towards the upkeep of the Plain but it is quite steep for anyone touring Sri Lanka on a budget. We got up at 5am to arrive for 6am. Unfortunately upon arrival the ticket machine was broken so we didn't end up getting going until 7:30am(ish).  We got very unlucky with the weather in that the fog didn't lift and so the view was none existent. It's also worth preparing your bag in advance. We hadn't planned to head up to the Horton Plains before we got to Nuwara Eliya, but decided to on arrival and arranged an early pickup (5am) with our tuktuk driver.  Nuwara Eliya is cold at that time of day,and we were very grateful for our padded jackets - make sure you prep well for a cold morning!  The journey over in the dark was, well, interesting - low-lying mist on the unlit roads, speeding drivers trying to overtake at all opportunities (it is Sri Lanka after all!) and low powered tuktuk lights all made for a memorable trip!  After buying our entry tickets ($45 for two people including all fees and taxes) we headed up to the trail head as the sun was coming up, with a few scattered deer out on the plains - fairly magical!  The hike itself is a circular, so you can head either clockwise or anticlockwise - most guides say to go anticlockwise, as you reach Little World's End before World's End but we opted for the latter and didn't regret it at all - it's slightly easier as you get a flattish finish, and you also avoid most of the crowds - once we'd headed out the only people we saw for the first 4km or so were the quicker hikers heading past us (not sure why, this is the sort of place that deserves you take your time to soak in the atmosphere!)  The early start was a killer at 4.30am, but seemed like a great idea now - the light is beautiful at that time of day and there's still the early morning frost on the ground and low-lying mist in the valleys.  Baker Falls are nice (but no Iguazu!) and the views from World's End and it's little brother are great, but for me the real winner was the hike and the scenery - just magical at that time of day, and we felt at times we were no longer in Sri Lanka but maybe south America!  While we didn't see much wildlife on the outward part of the hike we saw quite a bit when heading back after Little World's End - a couple of giant squirrels and a few purple-faced leaf monkeys enjoying a feed in the early morning sun - plus quite a few birds.  The round trip is around 9km or so, but we took our time enjoying the journey.  Very highly recommended if you're in Nuwara Eliya - indeed, probably the best thing you can do here IMO!

I didn't find this particularly taxing in terms of fitness, but there is a lot of picking your way over rocky and muddy paths, some quite steep. As advised we got there really early - make sure you allow about half an hour to queue for tickets, then drive the couple of miles more to the actual start of the trail (where there is a toilet and small cafe). You need to make sure you don't have any plastic bags, as they will be taken away at the gate, but plastic bottles are OK if the label is removed. It will be cold when you start (15 degrees when we left Nuwara Eliya at 5am, 12 degrees at the gate to Horton Plains at 6am), but once you start walking you will soon warm up, so only one extra layer is fine, and shorts would have been OK. We actually set off walking at 6.45. Shortly after the start you have a choice of which way round you go. We chose anticlockwise, but with hindsight, I think the clockwise route would have got us to World's End quicker. There is a map at the start, but few signs on the way. The terrain was tricky, with rocky paths to start, and a couple of streams to cross. It then got steeper, and much muddier, which slowed us up. Unless you've never seen a waterfall, don't waste time by diverting to Bakers Falls. It's good, but very much the supporting act, and you can always go back after you've been to World's End. We finally got to World's End at about 5 to 9, and were very fortunate indeed - literally within 5 minutes, the view had disappeared, the mist just rolling up the whole valley - quite a sight to see. So disappointing for anyone arriving after that, as there was nothing to see. The rest of the park is pleasant, but not spectacular. Further along the valley there is Mini World's End, but I can't tell you what the view would have been like! Once past these, the terrain becomes much flatter, apart from one fairly steep rocky path, and the mist doesn't encroach on the rest of the park. There's a toilet on the way back, on the edge of the hillside, open sided with a pretty decent view. I had walking shoes on, but on the way back we passed locals in flip flops!

As an obese person with a bad right knee and a recovering strained left upper thigh muscle, I was worried that I could not tak÷ on the challenge that was Horton's Plains, especially after reading horrifying reviews about it. Fortunately, all my fears were unfounded! Walking at a moderate pace, I found the walk entirely manageable though there were some tricky parts such as the rocky sections of the trail. On this note, do make sure to wear good shoes! We were also blessed as the weather conditions were in our favour. It did not rain the day before and neither did it on our hiking day. As a result, the paths were not very muddy and therefore easier to traverse. My friend and I, however, could see why the trail might be challenging should the weather be poor. A note on safety precautions to take, do not go too close to the edge of the cliff at World's End. According to our guide, a tourist had plunged to her death just a few weeks before our trip in an attempt to take a selfie. Some tips: 1. Check the weather forecast 2. It is preferable to have a guide since some paths may not be clear to the inexperienced 3. Bring some food and water 4. Do not bring plastic bags as there are thorough bagchecks before one enters the park 5. It is okay to bring bottled water into the park. However, do remove the plastic seal and label around the bottle before entering the park. 6. There are rubbish bins in the park. DO NOT LITTER. 7. Do not make too much noise as that might scare away wildlife. We had an unpleasant encounter with a group of noisy and rude tourists and had to ask them to tone it down. Do respect the environment and be comsiderate to others. That way, the walk will be pleasant for everyone! :) Overall, I enjoyed the trail as the views were lovely and it was certainly good exercise!

Our guide picked us up from our hotel at 05.00 and we munched on our hotel prepared packed breakfast as we drove to the park. I'm not a morning person but it was so worth the early start. A couple of practical tips. Get there early as the mists come in during the morning and the view from World's End is lost. It is a circular walk and I would recommend doing it in a counterclockwise direction which gives you the World's End later in the walk and prevents a steep hill finish back to the car park

Location;	Central province, Sri Lanka Nearest city;	   NUWARA ELIYA and OHIYA Coordinates	   6°48′N 80°48′ECoordinates: 6°48′N 80°48′E Established;   1969 (Nature reserve)1988 (National park) Governing body;	Department of Wildlife Conservation Horton Plains is a popular tourist destination, with World's End being the key attraction.The park is accessed by the Nuwara Eliya-Ambewela-Pattipola and Haputale-Boralanda roads, and there are railway stations at Ohiya and Ambewela.World's End is a sheer precipice with a 870 m (2,854 ft) drop.It is situated at the southern boundary of the park. Another cliff known as the Lesser World's End of 270 m (886 ft) is located not far from World's End.Baker's Falls, a waterfall formed by Belihul Oya, a tributary of the Walawe River is named after Sir Samuel Baker, a hunter and explorer  who attempted to establish a European agricultural settlement at Nuwara Eliya. The waterfall is 20 metres (66 ft) high. Slab Rock Falls is another well-known waterfall in the plains. The waterfall can be reached by walking on one of the main trails; the trail is a bit steep at the end but the difficulty level is medium to easy.

Getting to Horton Plains requires traveling on narrow windy roads. It took several attempts for our van to make it up one of the hair pin curves. This trek was included in our tour, our driver insisted we get in the car by 5am to start our walk by 6am so we don’t get stuck in the hectic traffic jam and the views would be clear from the mist. Let me tell you the drive to here and back to our hotel scared me, I’ve been driven in lots of countries and have desensitised myself to the crazy driving but this time I almost wet my pants. The Horton plains form an undulating plateau over 2000 meters high, which consists mainly of grasslands interspersed with patches of forest, with some unusual high-altitude vegetation. The plains are more often than not, visible only before 10.00am due to the heavy mist, which engulfs the area. The most unique feature of the Horton Plains is the "World's End". This is a sheer 1,000 feet vertical escarpment which visitors throng to see. The Horton Plains was once the hunting ground for Mr. Farr, a former British Governor which is today home to rare species of fauna and flora.

Horton Plains is a gently undulating highland plateau at 2,100.meters above sea level of Sri Lanka,lying at the south end of the central highlands. It is dominated by Kirigalpoththa (2.389 meters) to west and Totupolakanda (2,357 meters) to the north. Kirigalpoththa and Totupolakanda are the second and third highest mountains in Sri Lanaka. Tha charm of the plateau and encircling mountain range, often concealed mist, is enhanced by Baker's Falls and the two two escarpments, Small Worlds End (274 meters) and Big Worlds End (884 meters). The plateau is drained by tributaries of Mahaweli Ganga (main river of Sri Lanka) to the north (Agra Oya) and the Walawe Ganga to the south (Belihul Oya), serving as an important catchment area for these two rivers which have been harnessed for irrigation and hydro power. This plateau consists of many Amphibians, three types of harmless reptiles, birds and mammals including the leopard. Access to the plains are mainly from Ohiya, Pattipola and Nuwara Eliya. There are foot trails from Nagarak Trail is from the Agrapathana - Diyagama Tea Estate and also from Belihul Oya which falls into the same Nagarak Trail. This is place you must visit and possible to camp in the camping site. Plenty of Wildlife and ideal location for a wildlife photographer like me who is looking for adventure  .

We traveled from central nuwara eliya early in the morning and start  trekking around 6am. The plain is magical with mist and fog hanging high and low. Depending on luck you will spot a deer or two. You will hear all sorts of sound from the woods, birds, bugs, distant streams. The walk in general is quite easy, no major climb, mainly flat. Some areas are a little rocky, quite wet and slippery after rain/fog. On a steady pace the loop is about 3hours. Will highly recommend it to everyone. We had a very good time.

The views are amazing and well worth the 5 stars but the tracks around the area are more likely a 2 and in places very challenging and it appears that in June/July there are a lot of wash-aways which means you need to climb over boulders or walk in amongst what looks like stream beds. Do make sure that you get there early in the morning. We had to wait at little worlds end for the mist to lift but the wait was well worth it  for the view and then another challenging walk to Worlds End for even more amazing views. Toilets were really poor with broken doors, broken cisterns that made them almost unusable. A lot of the steps in the area were also badly washed away which is where the challenge comes into it.

I arranged a tuk-tuk with my homestay in Haputale to go here very early one mid-week morning. This cost 2500lkr, as the drive is over an hour and the tuk-tuk driver waited for 3hrs (return trip). Entrance to the park is expensive, probably too expensive, but there is no way of avoiding this. However, the circular 9km hike once you're within the park is very rewarding. The path is fairly challenging as there are a range of terrains, from sandy red coloured rocky river-bed style paths, narrow paths with 4000ft drops at one side, and flat ordinary trails along the plains. There is much wildlife to see, as well as the views. As for the plains, they looked not unlike the Yorkshire Dales in England, except with Rhododendron bushes! This area was a refreshing change of terrain from the endless yet beautiful hill views which are common in the area. Make sure you get there between 06:00 - 07:00 am to get the most out of the views. Cloud cover usually lifts at this time, then falls again a few hour later. Despite this, the views are only part of the experience. For me, the hike was the most enjoyable aspect of the visit, as well as the unusual early morning jungle sounds.

Everyone told us the best chance of seeing Worlds End (a view from the top of a cliff edge looking down into the valley of a small town which is picturesque) was to go very early in the morning. We were so tired from climbing Adam peak the following day and having no sleep we opted for a longer lay in so only got to Norton Plains as 7.45am. Saying that the weather that day wasn’t the best but it least it was dry. The 9km walk though was lovely. We basically had the whole park to ourselves (we saw maybe 20 people during our visit) and it was picturesque, beautifully quiet and the local wildlife were so used to people that they would come over to you or at least not run away when you approached. So did we get to see Worlds End? Unfortunately not, but whether we got up really early and chanced it or did what we did I think the chances for that day was limited due to the time of year. What I will say though is it didn’t take away the enjoyment we had of walking around the route, seeing the wildlife and experiencing the quietness. You will need to hire a driver and a jeep to get there as the roads aren’t great but most hotels will do that for you.

This is a national park and protected zone full of vegetation, water falls, lot of animals and birds, wonderful place for nature lovers and camping, I spent the whole day exploring the reserve, not to be missed if you on a holiday visiting Nuwara eliya.

The place is accessible only by private car and the road is steep and narrow, moreover its around 1.5 hour journey from Nuwara Eliya. Then the entrance ticket price is too high according to me, which along with car cost makees an expensive trp. But its worth it! The mountains, waterfalls, jungles and deers...all make it up for the money. Wear comfortable hiking shoes, and better to avoid if physically unfit. i would like more signs in the planes, we got lost a couple of times.

It’s a very early start because you need to complete the walk before it gets too hot. But, it’s very cold at 05:00 so wear layers: I wore two t-shirts, a hoody and a waterproof and de-layered as the sun started to rise. You need good walking shoes really. We saw a guy go over on his ankle (it’s quite rocky in places) and really struggle. Be very careful when you get to the World’s End viewing points. Lots of people perch on the edge doing yoga poses but it’s very dangerous. The wind can whip up from nowhere and someone has died there. Make sure you take a packed breakfast but don’t take any plastic. They check your bags as you go in and remove the labels from water bottles and the straws from juice cartons, which is to be applauded.

Its a nice place for walking. Along the way there are waterfalls. May not be ideal if you are with chidren. The walk to the world's end takes about 2-3 hours depending your speed. You also may see deers and other animals. Nice peaceful walk thru nature.

A visit to the Horton Plains should be a must for Tourists to enjoy the fresh air and nature at its best.    Walking, hiking, looking at the flora and fauna  is pure pleasure. If you love nature and some kind of walking, hiking this is ideal. Not suitable for elders who can't walk few Kms. So for hiking lovers this is a good one. It's just some walking. Not hiking. But need some strength. You have to buy tickets to enter. This is like a management fee. A small amount. Nature is so lovely and nice. It's so silent, Do not break the silence in here. If you are afraid of sunburn use sun cream, sunglasses and get some drinking water for your visit. along with a hat may be.

This a definite must visit if you are in the area. Very pretty scenery. In addition to the Plain itself, you can access Mini Worlds End, Worlds End and Bakers Falls via a hike. Keep at least 04-05 hours for the whole walk around the Plain if you hope to complete the full trail. Note - no plastic items are allowed inside the Plain.

Initially we were decidedly sceptical about putting going to Horton's Plains. There was not one, but many reasons for that. To go to Horton’s Plains one has to start early. In fact, as early as 5AM and for that we would have to wake up at least at 4AM. Not to mention the unbearable cold outside. On top of that, Horton plains had a lot of mixed reviews about the walks and the views it offered. All that too for a extravagant entrance fees. We were struggling with the thought of waking up that early and going out in the cold on a long walk where the possibility of views being completely blocked by the clouds was high. But then on the other hand, we did wish to go ahead with the plan, given that we had come all the way along. At the end, we did go there. After a drive of an hour and a half, we reached the entrance where we booked the tickets, and paid the cab entrance fees. Even at that time, the place was overly crowded with tourists and their vehicles. A heavy fog was around. We thought we were prepared for the cold. As suggested by a few blogs, I was wearing 5 layers of warm clothing. We got off the cab and went to join the long queue for the entrance tickets. The cold was unbearable and soon we were shivering. Thankfully the tickets were finally sorted out and we got back in the cab, to drive towards the entrance gate. The fog had slowly started to clear up as we started with the walk. It was a three hour closed trail, a simple trek with a little up and down slopes and a little rocky patches here and there. Nothing scary. The fog is basically created by cloud forests in the Horton’s plains. Luckily enough, the sun popped out of the clouds, clearing up the fog. The Baker’s falls offered a pretty view. We got clear, unhindered views form World’s end view point. What Luck! But then, the views were actually not that impressive. And the walk was not that challenging. I would like to mention one impressive thing about the management of Horton plains. At the entrance, they have a baggage check point where no tourist is allowed to proceed with a piece of plastic, may it be a bag or a bottle or a chewing gum box, thus keeping Horton plains plastic free. I think this is a very sensible step and ideally should be followed everywhere around the world.

Go there early, as early as you can, to beat the mist. Wear comfortable footwear and your bottles of water cannot be covered with paper. It's a lot of walking, climbing and will require you to be moderately fit. We did the whole shebang including the falls, and that took us about 3 hours. Once you arrive, you have two options, either to continue straight or go left, we went left. Our guide said we should reach the little and big world's ends before 9:30 so the mist doesn't settle in and he was right. If we had been 15 minutes late, we wouldn't have seen anything. The mist covered the whole area 5 minutes after we were done taking pictures. It was beautiful to see the cloudy body follow us and then cover us as we continued trekking throughout the planes. You can take a snack with you and eat it on top of big world's end, it's a beautiful place, cannot describe it in words. Really worth the visit and the workout !

The 9km route is relatively easy, with mostly flat terrain but a few patches of bouldering and climbing that does make it trickier in parts. Allow for about 3 to 3.5 hours if you stick to the path (we veered off a bit and extended our walk off the beaten track). The viewpoints are quite spectacular and the surroundings serene. A worthwhile excursion.

A great opportunity to enjoy the splendor of nature and spend the day actively! Wake up early, obligatory comfortable shoes,headcover, protective cream, sunglasses and drinking water. If you arrive early, you need a jacket, in the morning in early May it was cool. Before entering the territory of the reserve, a ticket office with a queue for 10 - 20 minutes. We were with a personal guide who took care of entrance tickets but you can go by  yourself (get lost if you do not turn off the way is impossible). There is a parking before the start of the route, where both the touristic and personal cars park. There is also a cafe that looks rather suspicious, but our guide said that it is possible to have a tea and eat traditional pastries. It was not bad! The toilet is located at the back of the cafe, it is better to visit it, because there are no more lavatories on the entire route. Despite the clouds during the entire walk and a fairly cool temperature in the morning in the first 2 hours, the noses and cheeks burned, so you must always apply a protective cream, then a walk of at least 9 km will be comfortable and enjoyable. The road in places is sometimes rather stony and difficult, therefore it is better to choose another occupation for children and people with limited motor abilities. The nature is amazing, the silence, the singing of birds and the murmur of water in streams, passing into small rivers and waterfalls are interrupted only by groups of passing tourists. Early in the morning saw one deer and several roe deer grazing not so far from the cafe. On the way there were chameleons and earthen small lizards, many birds. We did not hurry, we admired the surrounding nature for a long time, and after 6 hours we completed the ring of the route. A nice rest for everyone who is going to Horton Plains!

This was one of my highlights in Sri Lanka! The views are incredible! The walk is very enjoyable! Make sure to get there early so you can enjoy all the view before the mist rolls in! I would consider this a must if visiting Sri Lanka!

It was a lovely hike to view worlds end and mini worlds end. Loved the view. Would recommend bringing water, and wearing proper shoes. Also snacks! It s advised to go during early morning and not late evenings. The view is worth the climb.

Loved the loop hike. Go early to avoid crowd we were at the gate at 6. Really nice hike seeng World Ends, waterfall and nature at its best. Absolutely no plastic is allowed past the starting point and I am very impressed. They checked our backpacks and removed even plastic labels from water bottle! The hike was plastic free so I think it's a great idea!!

We left at 5:30 am from our hotel in nuwara Eliya to start our hike at 7am. The journey was around an hour in a TUK TUK (2500rps return journey) with 30 mins cueing. Most people come at this time to avoid peak heat and to see the views at worlds end without clouds. The route although not sign posted well can be done easily without a guide. Don’t worry there’ll be plenty of walkers around from all ages doing the walk at the ungodly hour. You can choose 2 routes: route 1 is the one to your left and goes straight when you reach it. This will take you to mini worlds end, worlds end and bakers fall in that order. Plus point - you’ll def get to the main attraction without clouds. Down side is you’ll have a harder trek back uphill. Route 2- this is the one we chose. The path when you reach the first bifurcation is the one going down the steps ahead of you. This will lead you to bakers falls, worlds end and mini worlds end in this order. Plus point - it’s an easier journey back as it’s mainly downhill returning. Down side - by the time we got to mini worlds end it was so cloudy we couldn’t see the view! Either way both routes are around 11 km loop. It’s relatively easy- just feels very long and you get hot! Took us 4 hours at a leisurely pace. Make sure you get your hotel to pack you a breakfast box so you can eat it when you’re having a break there. The cost of the ticket depends on how many of you are there in your group- the more of you going the cheaper it will be individually. For 2 of us it cost 3315 each ( including our TUK TUK drivers entrance). If you’re in Nuwara Eliya a visit isn’t complete without a hike in hortons plain. The view from worlds end is AMAZING!

its an amazing place to be. i was told that you need to be at the plains by 6 o'clock as soon as the park opens to have a quiet view of the trail and mother nature. leaving by 4.30 totally worth it. i reached in time and its not like no-one was there, but very few. totally enjoyes the sun rise and then the trail on the park is beautiful as well. do remember that it gets crowded by 10'ish and youight want to avoid that. its almost 8 kilometers trail and it takes around 3 hours very easily even when you are continuously walking. stay healthy ppl!!!

Horton Plains is worth visiting if you do enjoy a good hike. Also; the landscapes are beautiful and very different from what you'll see in other parts of Sri Lanka. It is a bit pricey though, and I wouldn't recommend visiting Horton Plains for World's End alone. If you're not that much into nature or walking: don't come here! You can see equally impressive or better views for free at other places in Sri Lanka and it'll save you the money and time to get there. People with mobility problems may find this hike less enjoyable, because the trail can be challenging in places and paths can get slippery after rainfall.

We arrived at 6am in order to walk to World's End before mist came down. We had a fantastic 10km walk and the views from World's End were truly stupendous. We saw a few birds but not much more by way of wildlife. Nonetheless, the walk was a highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka. There is a small exhibition and (paid) toilets. I was a bit miffed to see that the exhibition asks what damage you have done by visiting the park that day: if visitor numbers are such a concern, then perhaps pricing and entrance policies should be amended rather than passively criticising the people who have paid $25 for the privilege of visiting the park.

If you're into walking I would highly recommend the walk through Horton Plains to World's End! The scenery is beautiful! There are rolling hills, a beautiful waterfall and spectacular views from both World's End and Mini World's End. Tips: - Go early! The walk takes about 3 hours in total and about 1.5 hours from the starting Point to reach World's End (the main viewing point) We left our hotel in Newara Eliya at 5.30 and started walking at 7am. - Wear runners and comfortable clothes - I'd recommend layers (as it can be chilly at 7am and very warm by 9am). We were lucky with the weather but apparently it rains at lot so bring a raincoat). - Do the walk anti-clockwise! There's a main path from the carpark up to the start of the loop. At the sign board go straight ahead (most people to left). The first part of the walk is open to the elements so offers beautiful views as the sun rises and it's nicer to do this part of the walk when it's a little cooler (If you walk in the other direction there is little shelter from the sun as you're returning). Also there are less crowds at the waterfall!

The trek is around 10 km ... the place is around an hours drive from nuwara Eliya . Try and head out early cos if u r late the views at the worlds end would be covered in mist . We did the trek at the end of march the weather was pretty good . Carry a bottle of water and some light snacks as there is nothing available on the route inside . A small shop located outside sells water biscuits and basic Sri Lankan snacks

I was there with my family during the sinhala/tamil new year season. Perhaps due to season in Nuwara Eliya the park was absolutely crowded. Which we did not like that much but i think this is not something we can't avoid. However the park was spectacular as ever. weather was very kind to us in everyway. We had a perfect day.

We reached around 11.30AM  there as we were travelling from Kandy!! I went with two of my Sri Lankan friends and I felt foreign ticket is overpriced as no where close to them. It's around 9kms walk inside the forest which seems easy as nature at its best. First we saw Mini world end and 500mts above world end and scenery is stunning. Best time to go is before afternoon as mist will be covered after that. Best thing is Bakers waterfalls which is beautiful and don't feel like moving out from there. Stunning view all-around the walk. It was raining heavily half through our walk but we continued walking in the rain. Spend enough time inside as nature beauty is amazing. Take enough water during the walk. Wear shoes as most of the rocks are slippery. Take umbrella in case of rain as there is no shades inside the forest.

We went to the park from the Heritance Tea Factory Hotel where we set off at 0445 to get there before the park opened at 0600. Dawn was breaking on a misty morning. We were soon joined by other vehicles but an early star is recommended to avoid the heat. Paths are a bit rough and were pleased we wore proper hiking shoes. It is very hilly but the views are well worth it, Expect to take 5 - 6 hours of hard walking. Our guide took us to Baker Falls which was a good place to cool off with the spray from the falls.

We got up at 4.30 to arrive extra early to spend several hours walking through the national park and to see mini world's end and world's end.  Incredible scenery, wildlife and dramatic cliff like drops.  Such a nice relief from the hustle and bustle of the rest of the island and such wonderful respite from the shocking litter everywhere else.  At least here we could appreciate the outstanding beauty of the island without extraordinary levels of litter and marketing hoardings.  Wear suitable walking boots/shoes.

As I live in Sri lanka for couple of months already I do know the prices around. Horton Plains was on my list since I'm a nature lover. However even though I went there with a local, at the entrance they have tried to overcharge even him for the simple fact of being with me,a "foreigner",they have asked somewhere close to 6000 rupees only for one person! We got really pissed as the entrance fee kept changing from 4200 to 7000 in just 5 minutes. In the end we left really annoyed and found other peak to climb. There are many other places around that area that are still so beautiful and for free so don't let yourself being fooled just for a few hrs walk! P.S. We managed to see different  birds and even plenty of monkeys everywhere else we went around there, is not just Horton Plains that has it so spare your money if you can.

I would give this a 5 stars but there are a couple of reasons that made this not quite the ultimate experience. Let me give you the reasons why you SHOULD go: This simply a nice and breathtaking park. The scenery is lovely, the trail is nice, the hike is very easy and the park is very strict on littering policies. What you should know before you plan on going: Plan in advance and get there EARLY. The drive from Nuwara Elyia was at least an hour. We were told that if we wanted to see World's End (the nicest view of the valley) we needed to do the first half of the hike before 10 am because after that it's so cloudy you won't see anything. Also the big tours start at 7:30 am and the trails are crowded with people. So you basically need to be there when the park opens at 6am. So if you have an hour drive to do.... you need to leave at 5am.... you get the picture. The line at the entrance of the park was insane. We had to wait at least 30 minutes to get out tickets. The first part of the trail was nice, but after an hour or so, it started to get crowded...A LOT. I will sound mean but, WHY in hell do people think it's OK to go in NATURE to see animals and scenery and YELL and blast their MUSIC on their phone for everyone to hear? The park itself was beautiful, but the tourists ruined the whole experience for me. This place has become a big touristy attraction and the amount of people being disrespectful was insane. It's my opinion but the park should limit the amount of tourists they let in at a time.

Horton Plains is a great place to discover Sri Lanka's outdoors. Rare cloud forest, open plains, waterfalls and a terrific view off of World's End viewpoint (only in the early morning) all in the easy highland climate. We were lucky having been guided by Nimal, the most knowledgeable guide we met in our 3 week stay in Sri Lanka. He has abundant knowledge of flora and fauna (explained to us plenty of plants and showed us animals), but also of all the other things we wanted to learn about (any place or thing in) Sri Lanka. Thanks to his great English, we have learned a lot during this half day trip of the Horton Plains. He is smart, helpful and kind, you felt like he's always got your back and he knows exactly what tourists like! Thank you Nimal for making this trip such a good experience!

Horton Plains National Park is a good place to visit even though the entrance fee is quite high and service is poor. We arrived at the gate at 6 am (just open) and there were already many people. The 9 km walk is not difficult and there is a lot to see and to hear when other visitors keep quiet which is not always the case. Park authorities should use some of the money they receive to improve ways and toilets!

We love our morning at hortain plains Go early .Did the Horton plains trekking. Beautiful views so worth a visit. Well preserved by staff ... check your bag for plastic packaging as dropping of litter strongly discouraged. .. It's easy to follow the path. Best time to visit early morning late afternoon as it's a good 5 miles on the circular route very nice beautiful place location was superb

Are you sick of all the rubbish too? We often thought, man, why dont they do something about that and protect at least some landscapes? Here, however, they do. And that was the first impression we got from the park itself. The private booked drive up here from nuwara eliya was about an hour long and pretty curvy, but alright. On the entrance the staff checked all our bags for rubbish and asked to throw it away. The walk was awesome, not only because of the weather, but also because of the great welcoming by a majestic dear right on our way! The countryside invites to take Photos and rest in a quiet surrounding. The worlds end was pretty impressive, even the 'little' one. The big one... well, you got to see it yourself! But take care, its a long way down there. The whole walk ended with a beautiful waterfall... wow, what a day! I tell you, it is totally worth it. We've been for five weeks in sri lanka, and this was one of our favorite trips. The quitness and peace up there is something you dont find in sri lanka at every corner. However, here a tip: Pack your food in boxes or paper and Your drinks in bottles (not those tetra packs). Otherwise you'll get to throw it away at the entrance.

One of my key highlights of Sri Lanka trip !  Totally enjoyed the hike - was initially worried that it might be too strenuous but it was manageable.  Recommend to go early to catch sunrise and the fantastic view.  Be prepared for the change in weather too - Low temp in the early morning and hot humid temp in mid/ late morning.

Our group went to the Horton Plains for a recommended hike leaving our hotel early in the morning when it was very misty.  However this is a good time to start the trek but beware it can be quite cold so be prepared for some cold and wet weather.  It is lovely trek of approximately 9k and is not very difficult if you are quite fit and used to walking.  The scenery is amazing especially at the summit (The Worlds End) and the overall views beautiful. Did not see much wildlife but not sure I expected to as there is a significant number of people on the trek.  It is well worth doing just for the trek and the scenery.

I went with a driver who helped buy my ticket and showed me the way and then I hiked around the trial by myself. The hike is about 9 km and since I stopped to take photos it toom almost 3 hours. The path is easy to follow and as long as you have an average fitness level you should havr no problems. There are a few areas where you will be walking down/up a path that has rocks in the way or tree roots (the tree root area was the steepest). The path to Baker's falls is stairs. The scenery is worth the hike and going early in the morning is a good idea as its usually the clearest time. Side note: its a but chilly (12 C) in the early morning and most people wore a jacket for at least the beginning part of the hike

Unbelievable place.... Today the weather was amazing and it started to rain after 2 pm, heavily rain... you need a hiking boots specially if there is a chance for raining ... but you don't need a guide, all the road marked and you can easily recognise the walking routes, take enough drinking water with you for about 4 hours, tissue, and something to keep mosquitos away from you, there is a special wet wipes for that, if you like to explore it more just incase buy a map for the park from the entrance office or print it out from Google maps, it's even much better, I used it Today. Great experience, if you did not explore Horton plains while you are in Sri Lanka, you really waste your time and money!

The Nationalpark is very clean, people working there take care that you do not litter. Which I think is a great spirit. The walkaround to go to the different sites can be done in 2-3 hours, depending on how fast you walk and how long you linger at the different spots. If you go in the mornings, which you should do since otherwise the fog will come in from the coast, there is a big queue at the entrance. You have to queue approx. 20 - 30 minutes. And then there are of course a lot of tourists on the walk around, but that´s to be expected. Nevertheless it is beautiful and worth it.

This was without doubt one of our favourite trips in Sri Lanka. We left Nuwara Eliya at 5:00 to get there early enough to beat the crowds and heat. Our driver came with us as he understandably preferred walking around a beautiful national park over sitting in his car. This was good as he provided some snippets of information and history and told us his preferred route around (left/clockwise) We particularly enjoyed little world's end as it was quieter and had equally amazing views. If visiting Sri Lanka this should be a must do as the scenery is incredibly beautiful.

One thing I loved about this walk is that there are no guard rails- walkers were responsible for their own welfare. Plastic was confiscated at the entrance.  We had some small fruit in a plastic bag which they transferred into a paper bag. I had trouble breathing while doing the climbs, but thoroughly enjoyed the walk as a whole.

The circular trail is 8km long and on average takes 3 hours to complete which allows time for a breakfast picnic / photographs / simply admiring the views. There is no need for a guide and I'm not even sure they are available such is the trail so easy to follow. An early start is required as apparently the cloud comes in daily mid morning onwards. Very enjoyable and not too taxing - we're in our 50s!

This place needs your early morning attendance. If you are a mountain person and love to trekking - this is the place for you. Just gear up with sports shoes and joggers. It has mini world ends and all beauty surrounded with mountains and fog.

Everyone crowds here at about 6am - seemingly after about 10 the clouds come in and you can't see much. The views are stunning from worlds end, and a great place to sit and eat a picnic breakfast. The walk itself is fairly obvious, some slightly tricky bits up and down rough terrain so wear sturdy footwear and take water etc. It's about 10k for the whole round trip, and it took us about 2.5 hours including a 20 minute sit down at worlds end for breakfast. Some groups of families/older travellers were moving slower and will probably take 3-4 hours. Other than worlds end there is "little worlds end", which is exactly what you'd expect, a waterfall which is worth a look, and a walk through pleasant rolling jungle and the plains. The paths aren't perfectly finished and can be uneven for quite long distances, but they're obvious to follow and you won't need a guide. All in all, a good half day.

We visit Horton Plains as part of a Sri Lankan Wildlife tour and hiked the circular route taking in mini World's End, World's End and Baker falls.  It was an excellent hike over some challenging terrain (narrow rocky river beds downhill).  Thankfully we'd read our itinerary notes and were fully prepared with hiking shoes, apparently a number of visitors had not.  How they managed the 3 hour walk in flip flops was beyond me!! The views from mini World's End and World's End are spectacular albeit there were a lot of people there.  The lack of any safety railing of course was splendid as it did not spoil the view but was a little disconcerting for those of us that aren't keen on really high cliffs!  Deer and stags to be seen on the plains, very close up which was lovely.  Birds to be heard - not necessarily seen though - did spot some small ground squirrels and a couple of lizards.  Toilet facilities interesting at the start of the park - you are definitely open to the elements!  Overall a great experience and fantastic walk in the natural environment of this beautiful country.

It's more than 9km trail that passes through waterfalls, clouds and dense forests. Carrying enough water is the key and don't try to do it at noon or with kids or elderly people. Fees is 3k lkr for foreigners. It's safe and an amazing experience. Key attractions are waterfall, world's end.

Apparently, everyone includes this on their trip to Sri Lanka! Trekkers, birders, tourists. I couldn't understand why we were being overtaken by jeeps, tuc tucs, bikes, buses at 5.45 am. Only as we neared the entrance did we realise what was going on. It was like Piccadilly Circus in the rush hour only worse. Our jeep was packed in with every other mode of transport and we had to wait for about an hour or longer for our guide to collect a ticket from the ONE booth that was open. Absolute chaos. Even when we eventually got into the park having eaten our packed breakfast from the hotel, there was no organised car parking at the other end so I can't say that I particularly enjoyed the experience. We walked along the tracks as we were birding but even then you had to ensure you weren't wiped out by the jeeps steaming along. Unless you're going for the trekking then I wouldn't bother!

The walk was superb and great fun, although you need a reasonable level of fitness and (suggest) sensible footwear as the path can be a bit undulating and uneven in places. Total cost for 2, including the car was just short of 7000 Rupees but remember you need to add the cost of whatever form of transport you use to get to the Plains. It’s a long way by car from Nuwara Eliya - c 1.5 hours on a bumpy road each way but well worth it for the view from Worlds End. Aim to get there as early as possible eg be at the start of the Plains walk by 7 am to try to avoid the crowds - many of which simply meander and moan about the terrain. The view when you get to Worlds End is inspiring, but make sure you are at the edge by 1000 hrs as the rain forest clouds quickly rises up from the valley below and covers everything in a moist haze. Plan carefully and leave early and you will have a fantastic experience
