Horton Plains National park is located in the hill country of Sri Lanka. It is not very accessible as the roads are narrow and steep. A payment has to be made to visit the park and the price for 2 adults at the local rate wa approx. Rs. 600.  When we visited the customer service centre on the premises we were informed that we should pay the rate for foreigners which was Rs. 3000 each, although we were born in Sri Lanka and spoke the national language fluently.  The women at this centre were extremely aggressive and threatened to take us to court if we did not pay this grossly over-priced rate. The entire conversation took place in Fluent Sinhalese and we showed them our place of birth as Colombo, Sri Lanka on our Australian passports. One of the women even attempted to snatch the passports away from us.  We therefore reluctantly paid the higher rate, after further argument, for the sake of peace. The males at this centre were quite amenable and were in agreement with us rather than the women. We strongly believe that this money found its way into their pockets.

We went on the hike, as many people do, early in the morning (6.30). We walked the whole circuit. There were a huge queue of minibuses at the ticket entrance. They are strict on what can be taken onto the plain, so don’t take plastic bags (bottles are fine but they strip off their plastic wrapper) as they will be confiscated during your bag search at the entrance to the walk. If the sun comes out you will need sunscreen as the sun is strong at altitude. We did not see any toilets at the visitor's centre or car park. You will need sturdy trainers and water. You can do the walk in around 3 hours, more if you like to stop to admire the scenery and take photos. Not all the route is an easy path, eg. some boulders to climb over, but we are not big trekkers and found it manageable. There is a waterfall (Baker's Falls), quite a difficult but short climb up to it. If you take the right hand path first on your walk you will do this near the beginning or if you take the left hand path first you will do this ear the end if you do a circular route. We didn’t see any monkeys but heard their calls on a couple of occasions. We saw a few birds, not as many as expected, and a colourful lizard.

the Horton Plains National Park is simply stunning. The 10km round trip hike, including the Worlds End lookout point took us about 3 hours with lots of stops along the way. Beautiful scenery and wildlife. The path was quite rough in parts and definitely not suitable for those with mobility issues

We were advised to start the walk as early as possible I.e. sunrise around 6.30am in order to see the mini and end of the world viewpoints before it is hidden in the clouds. However we only started the trek at 9.30am but we were so lucky. We took the clockwise route, going to mini world first, end of world second and the waterfalls last. We actually saw both end of the worlds just in time, with literally minutes spare before the cloud obliterated everything. Take water with you, good walking boots as it can be slippery in places after rain. There are some rocky patches to go through but although it can be strenuous at times, it is not that difficult. Also by going early you avoid the higher temperatures later in the day. From the first junction,  we took 3 hours and it was a really enjoyable trek. It is well marked, and if in this area this is one excursion not to be missed.

We went to Horton Plains wanting to take a hike. I was aware it wouldn't be a real hike (boots, stones, steep ground) but actually we didn't feel at all the difference of altitude. It was like a walk in a different park. The most interesting thing is that you can feel the big difference of temperature and moist when you go from the plains into the forest, and vice versa. We got up on World's End when the mist already was there, but the view was amazing!

The Rough Guide to Sri Lanka describes this hike as "walking in a few gentle hours".This description is highly misleading: The walk is 9 km, some of it climbing, some on rough trails that are closer to dry river beds, where one steps from rock to rock. The hike took me about three and a half hours, and I was exhausted at the end, especially as the climb down, then back up from Baker's Falls, is in the final third of the walk. The scenery is very beautiful, and at World's End utterly gorgeous, though there are few animals to be seen, except for several Samba deer in the parking lot! Even the drive up to the park, in the early morning, with the hills and trees tops poking through the clouds, is beautiful. However, words of warning: pack lots of water, and additional provisions to the breakfast your hotel would have given you - you will need to nourish yourself during the trek. And  consider your level of fitness: I saw a lot of exhausted looking older people.

This was a most enjoyable circular walk although the terrain and weather (it started off being cool and damp but brightened up to be like an early summer's day in the UK)  rather reminded me of Shropshire! We didn't go early but in some respects that was no bad thing as we met people who had had to wait ages to get a ticket. The circular walk that most people follow takes in a range of terrains, and it can be rough underfoot: good walking shoes are an advantage here. Take a few hours to enjoy the scenery. I reached World's End after the mist had rolled in so I didn't get to see the spectacular views; though I was enchanted by the cloud forest which is the natural alternative. Definitely worth the effort to visit this place, though don't expect to be alone - it's popular.

The day and time came perfect, with a light shower of drizzle and mist intermittently, giving it the right balance of coolness, the foggy outfit and the adventurous feeling that you are seeing the unseen. The park gate opens at 7am but there is a one hour long que to buy tickets at the entrance. The last 2 km of the road is in really bad shape so expect a bumpy ride. This walk was one of the highlights of my solo trip around Sri Lanka. We started out at 5:45am, under clear skies and a full moon. We were the 4th car to arrive, and watched the sun rise within the park. It was so beautiful, as the full moon and sun rise was at one stage in line with each other. The sky was so clear I felt I could touch the stars. The walk was easy, and as I have a dodgy knee, was glad of this. We took a different path,inadvertently,  upon reaching mini world's end. It was overgrown, and followed the edge of the mountain, but the views were spectacular. And we were the only walkers, although a couple did follow us, we did not see them until we reached Worlds End. We enjoyed breakfast here, and the sky was clear, with an amazing view down to the valley below. The weather was perfect, and we managed to stay clear of all the other tourists. At times we were the only ones on the track. It was so peaceful, and so beautiful. I would definitely recommend leaving at 5:45am from Nuwara Elliya, then you will definitely get to see the sunrise inside the park, and get some great photos. It was a very special time, and a wonderful walk.  I just wanted to enjoy nature, and the experience. After all, it is the journey, not the destination that is important.  I took this hike, with no expectations whatsoever, and was richly rewarded with my experience.

Our guide, Mike, explained that the walk was quite strenuous with a lot of uneven paths, etc.  Being fairly regular walkers, however, we found it relatively straightforward, although there is a degree of ascent which in the heat of the day did raise a sweat! We took the anti-clockwise route - from the visitor centre to Baker’s Falls then on to World’s End and then Mini World’s End before returning to the visitor centre.  The path is simple to follow, well signposted, with very little chance of losing your way. It took about 2.5 hours, including a stop at all three locations noted above. Assuming you don’t have mobility issues, we’d thoroughly recommend this as a worthwhile experience. The view from World’s End alone is worth the effort (assuming the clouds are on your side)!

The popular thing to do in this park is arrive at 6 a.m. and do the walk to World's End (about 9K  to do the full loop which also includes mini World's End and Baker's Falls) in order to see the view before the mist rolls in. However we had been told that it is so popular that the road in and out is non-stop traffic jams, and the trail is very crowded with hundreds of other walkers. So we decided to go in the early afternoon. Sure enough we could not see the view, but the walk - with very few other walkers - was beautiful, peaceful, still lots of birds to see, we had Baker's Falls to ourselves. Just gorgeous. And in late afternoon we had some wonderful views of the deer all to ourselves. One of my all-time favourite walks.

Most hikers will do this in three or less.  With two kids and taking our time at World's End, it took us four.  Sightings of sambar deer near the park entrance, and purple faced monkeys (big ones) on the hike.  Leopards are said to inhabit the park but with the large number of tourists, its not surprising that none were sighted.  The view from World's End are spectacular.  Hiking shoes are better, but we saw people with flip flops and business shoes as well.  There are some rocky patches that require good footwear.  The challenge is the early departure from your hotel, as you need to get into the park early enough to make World's End by around 9:00, as after the mist can come in and take way the great view.  Highly recommended.  Altititude is over 2000m

I've read reviews which have said it's not worth the effort but if you fancy a hike and don't mind getting up early I think worlds end is a good option. What I'd say up front is that I'd read in several places (e.g. lonely Planet) that this is an easy walk. It's not. As previous reviewers have mentioned, it's very up and down and the terrain is very difficult in places. For the elderly or infirm it would be impassable. I'm a relatively fit 50 something and I certainly built up a sweat! We were lucky in that we didn't arrive until around 10am as we had an accident in the van on the way. Sri Lankan's drive like lunatics, particularly the bus drivers and the rule seems to be that it's the responsibility of the person coming the other way to take avoiding action. We had an altercation with a motorcyclist overtaking on a blind bend which held us up for over 2 hours while waiting for police and insurance person. Anyway, I digress. It was a lovely day and we set off after 10 in bright warm sunshine. We decided to take the right hand Orion as most people were going the other way. It's roughly 6km going this way and 3km coming back on the other side of the loop. That's not what the sign says, which makes it equi-distant either way. Personally, I'd do it this way again as it meant that the walk back after worlds end was shorter. We were lucky in that when we arrived at Worlds end after 11.30, the view was reasonable clear. Not crystal but we could see past the lakes at Udalawale. The views on the way up to Horton's Plain were also fantastic I have to say. I'd echo the others comments about the Chinese groups. The peace and quiet was blissful when out of earshot. So do it if you're energetic and don't mind contributing the equivalent of about GBP15 to the environmental upkeep of the area.

While we were commenting most tourists places in Sri Lanka had an expensive entrance fee, Horton Plains (HP), was worth the cost. Such a serene and wonderful place to spend walking leisurely for 3 hours in the morning. It wasn’t a hard walk at all (these are subjective). It was leisurely pace, taking in the beauty of all the sights. Bakers fall and world end were truly magnificent. When we came to the fork where you had to choose your route to do Hp, we choose to go right. Do the right option if you want to avoid the crowds and loud tourists groups. Handful of people walking this side allowed us to take photos without disturbance and enjoy the morning walk. We left our hotel at 5am and got to the ticket counter at 6am on the dot. Even at that time, there were about 30 people ahead of us. Counters open at 6am. We got our tickets at 6:45 and got to the park at 7am(another 10 Min ride from the ticket counter) We booked a taxi that had our bags as we were continuing the journey onwards to Ella. One of our best mornings in Sri Lanka.

For 3500 rupee one would expect more. We did not manage to see any wildlife that were touted to roam the plains. The terrain was extremely rough and weather was hot and dry like a desert. Toilets were extremely filthy and not usable at all. Huge let down and gets a thumbs down.

This is a great walk of about 9KM with some beautiful scenery. Leaving the hotel at 5am is definitely worth it as it started to get really hot towards the end of our walk and got some great pictures of the sunrise on our way up to the car park. There were points where it was a little busy but overall we didn't see much of other people. Luckily our guide went ahead to buy our tickets whilst we were in the traffic jam entering the park so we could just walk straight in. Obvious highlight was seeing the sambar deer which was not at all startled by our presence. Well worth the trip as it was not something I'd thought I'd experience when in Sri Lanka.

We started at 5am from Nuwara Eliya to the Horton Plains by a shared Taxi (Cost 2500 for 2 persons, total 5k) the Horton Plains are real untouched nature. But the circle trip is ready to go for everybody. there are marks to follow and the much people at the first moment spread in the area. So you are feeling this nature and lovely place for yourself. We have taken 3h with some sidesteps and relaxing moments. but I think you could enjoy it longer or be much faster in hikking. Think the average is like 2,5h-3h. recommended!

The track on this hike is severely washed out in sections. It is an 8.9 km hike around the total loop to include Bakers Falls. I set off at 09.00 going clockwise around the loop, and with a brief stop at Mini Worlds End, I got to Worlds End at 10.00am. I got to enjoy the view for 15 minutes, and then watched the cloud move up the valley for 10 minutes, until it came up the cliff and engulfed the lookout. No view to speak of after that, but certainly an experience. If you have any difficulty in walking, I strongly recommend Lipton's Seat instead. It also has great views, and what you save on entrance fees will pay for  tuctuc to the top, with no walking or steps to do.

Maybe it's because, living in Northern California, I have close by some of the greatest landscapes in the world.  But I thought Horton's Plain, although quite nice, didn't quite live up to the hype.  The hike, about 10 kilometers, is very beautiful and you go through some pretty countryside, including some unusual rhododendron forests.  World's End, hyped to be the most amazing view in the world, was nice and you could see a long way, but I wouldn't get up this early, drive this far and walk this far to see it.  There is a nice waterfall, but I've seen better, right there in Nuwara Eliya.  But it's great that Sri Lanka is protecting places like this and bravo for that!  Now, maybe they could re-introduce some elephants, which roamed these plains years ago.  Now THAT would be worth all the hassle in getting here by 6am.

A challenging walk of around 6 miles including some steep scrambles up and down, but well worth it for the views and wildlife. Can be a long queue to enter - surely it should be possible for guides and drivers to buy tickets beforehand?

Your day starts at 5am with a car trip to the park.$50 per couple to get in 4500rp for a ride up there .Queue for 40 mins to get your tickets and finally arrive in the park.Packed with loud tourists.....Do not take cigarettes,lighters,plastics of any kind bar water bottles with the labels removed.This is to keep the park clean and rubbish free.If you do have things taken off you they will put them away until you get back and mark your tickets.When you reach the map go left rather than right as everyone seemed to go right to worlds End.If you go left you arrive there before the hoardes and can get your photos and GET OUT.People have no idea about noise levels and just spoil it for others.We had a crowd of Chinese turn up and ruin the whole experience with yelling at each other,throwing rubbish and getting in everyone’s way of taking photos.They all went right.Luckily Going the opposite way meant we basically had the track to ourselves a lot of the time.Beautiful views and not too hard a walk.A lot of locals turned up around 10.30 to start their trip which seemed like a great idea as everyone was basically finished by the time they arrived.Dont think you will get there for the sunrise as the queue to get your tickets makes you too late for that.Leaving late seems to be a better option and it wasn’t a hot walk even at 10.30am

This is a good thing to do in the area, a 9km walk with lots to see. The Worlds End was a really great highlight but get your timings right. First, the practical stuff. You will read that you need to get to Worlds End by 10.00 if you don't want to run the risk of cloud rolling in. We got there at 9.45 on a foggy morning and the clouds parted just in time but as we got around to Mini Worlds end (basically the same view) the clouds were coming in. To do this we left our hotel (Heritance Tea Factory 30 mins north of Nurawa Eliya) at 5.30. It's 1 HR from NE so we got there about 6.50. When you get to the back of the vehicle queue, leave the driver and walk (about 500m in our case) past the queuing cars to the ticket sales on the left. We had to queue - it was very slow moving with 1 counter only. You get there in the end (40 mins for us). Buy tickets for you (3,500 rupees each) and 1 for the driver (60 rupees), it will come as 1 ticket which you get stamped opposite and keep. By this time your vehicle should have reached you. I have no idea why people said you needed passports - we didn't. This may seem a long wait but it serves to spread the walkers out! You then drive another 2 km to the start of the walk. 1 further tip is to turn right at the Y junction as most people go the other way. It's very well signed and you can't go wrong and the walking seemed easier. Alternatively, go later, there is no queue at all at the ticket sales after 10 but you run the risk of cloud spooling the view.

It took us a while to decide whether to go on this hike or not. Getting up at 4:30, taking an hour ride to stand about an hour more at the ticket office - all in almost zero visibility, didn't give us any hopes for a good day. Things have changed once we entered the park though. We were probably lucky, but clouds and mist were gone and we had a super shiny sun for the whole day (take sun block with you!). Took the left path of the loop, reached Little World end first and went up the hill (the official road takes you around the hill). There you get to an amazing platform with much less people than the Big World End and a better view. Baker falls are worth of another 1-1.5h easy hike.

I can only review my experience and I would not recommend it. For a start you have to pay. 3500LKR each or about £17 in English money As I visited in February there is no chance you’ll see the sunrise from the park as it’s not open early enough, and even if it was, you wouldn’t beat the queue anyway -ticket office opens at 6am and we arrived at 5:45 to get in line (about the time of sunrise in February) If you get to the ticket office after 6am - the queue is large We did not see any animals here apart from maybe a handful of birds The view is nice, but it’s not so rewarding to get up at 4am in the cold - only for it to really warm up while you’re halfway round and you have to end up carrying half your clothes. The walk took 3 hours - we are healthy adults ages around 30. I wouldn’t recommend doing this. Instead I would get a Tuk Tuk to about 1km from the entrance, sit there and watch the sunrise and appreciate nearly the same view as you would get, but be left with more money in your pocket and a lot more energy and actually being able to see the sunrise instead of waiting in a queue for the time you could have seen the sunrise. Oh, for those of you who smoke, you can’t smoke there either.

The 9 Km trek that you can do here is not easy. We found it ok as experienced walkers, but beware if you're not fit! The security guards will check any obvious picnic bags for plastic and will remove it all, so hide the picnic in a rucksack or take put the plastic yourself! No catering on the site.

A very early start is needed to get to the ticket office for 07.00. The queues of cars is ridiculous and so is the queue to buy a ticket. There is only ever one ticket office open   It is very expensive (£37) for 2 people. You walk around a well defined walk, it is definitely better to go to baker falls first as there is slightly less walking uphill. The views throughout the 9km walk are stunning but remember there are no safety barrier at worlds end or little worlds end

My wife and I were contemplating whether to go, but we overcame the very early wake up (4:30am) for one incredible experience. While the hike was long and at points busy with tourists, World’s End is an absolute must if you’re in the area. It truly does feel like you’re at the end of the world. The park hosts extensive wildlife, including birds, monkeys and Sambal deer. The drive up to the plains is long and quite incredible. Be sure to go early and have a driver or guide planned for the day. We ate breakfast at World’s End so we could beat the crowd. If you’re bringing food, the park employees will ensure that it is not wrapped in plastic that will litter the park. If so, they will put it in a separate paper bag.

We arrived early in the morning and there where tons and tons of minivans taking tourist to the track to see sunrise. As the que was so long for the tickets that are unreanoably expensive, we saw the sunrise from the little van that smelled like disel. So to see the sunrise you have to start walking 5 in the morning latest because the main sight is Worlds End and you have to hike like an hour to get there. On the track there where A LOT of people so it felt like being in an airport. Van rent 4500, tickets 3500 per one person, so I’d think about going twice.

One of the main local tourist attractions, not to be missed.  As we were told, we made sure to be at the Park's entrance gate at 6.00 AM sharp, when it opens.  There was already a queue by then, and it was all a bit bureaucratically cumbersome and not cheap to get in.  Make sure to bring the exact amount of money (giving change money can be difficult if everybody pays with 5000 bills).  Make sure to wear proper walking shoes!   Was it all worth it to get-up that early for, and to endure the many other tourists groups (some of whom were irritatingly loud):  yes, I think so.  Didn't find the hike through the park and on the plains itself particularly interesting, but the highlights are clearly the sunrise in the mountains on the way up (already before arriving at the gate), and the spectacular mountain views from "Mini World's End" and "World's End" shortly after sunrise (when the skies are still clear, before the daily clouds are rolling-in blocking the vistas).  Included in the loop is Baker's Falls, quite some waterfall.  Not suitable for small kids, elderly or handicapped, walking a 9 km loop doesn't sound a lot, but it's quite some hike going up and down on sometimes slippery grounds (after a day of rainfall).  If you have them, bring your foldable mountain hiking sticks, very usefull we had those with us here!

Very strict when it comes to plastic, but no park ranger tried to stop the tourists from feeding the deer. When you try to 'conserve' this is part of it too. Shame. Note: Early wake-up, it's total madness when arriving at the park entrance. Getting out of the van to buy tickets, vans everywhere. Really chaotic, not organized, really Sri Lankan like I guess. We enjoyed watching this.

Up early to get to the gate for just after 6am. Bit of a queue, standing in the cold, but not too bad. From there it's a 3km drive into the park proper. There's a check for plastic and cigarettes, which other than bottled water, are not allowed into the park. After a short leg, there is a loop to take in the main sites. Most people go clockwise, we went anticlockwise, which made the start of the walk quite peaceful. Short diversion to Baker's Waterfall; OK but nothing special. World's End is a dramatic spectacle. Huge drop, with no barriers, so needs a bit of care with all the people about. We caught some wildlife - giant squirrel, purple faced monkeys and some birds, including Sri Lanka white eye. No deer. It's a 7 km walk over fairly rough ground as the path is more like a river bed, so decent shoes are recommended. Overall I was a bit disappointed, perhaps because of the cost of the whole thing, for what is a fairly straightforward excursion on one very busy trail. There is a walking trail to Kirigalpotta, the 2nd highest mountain in Sri Lanka, which may have been a better option. It's 14km in total. The park could do with more marked trails to give other options for those wanting to do more than the World's End loop and have guided walks to help see the wildlife.

We’d heard so much about the Horton plains that we had to do the (nearly) 10km walk. We didn’t get up ultra early as often recommended and  y Wife and I arrived at 8.30am to beautiful blue skies. Parked entrance fee including a small fee for the car and our driver was Rs 69,120 (about USD 45). Geez we wanted to see the park not buy it. None the less off we went and no sooner entered the park than we saw a magnificent Deer. Wonderful we thought, what a great sign of things to come - alas, never saw another specimen of wildlife. The walk was tricky in places. Lots of boulders, eroded creek beds, tree roots, uphill and downhill climbs but nothing any regularly fit person could not tackle. There were really only three spectacles to see. The mini worlds end. This was a look out into the valley below and we got there just as clouds and mist were starting to roll in. Beautiful. The next was worlds end. Supposedly more of the latter but the mists and clouds had rolled in and we could not see anything. The third was a water fall. Not the most spectacular I had ever seen but very pleasant. All in all some nice exercise but as a spectacle - left a lot to be desired. Would I recommend it. Not really unless you’re going just for the exercise. Many more beautiful places all over the world and in our own home country of Australia.

Most people visit Horton Plains to hike to World's End. If that's your goal, leave early. The clouds start to build up around 9:30, and after that, the view will be obscured. First you need to buy tickets to enter the park. That is a chaotic event itself, but eventually you will get your tickets. Many cars are there at 6am, when the park opens, so there will be a line. Don't be dismayed by fog in the early morning hours. The sun will fry it away in an hour or so. During our drive to the start of the trail, we saw sambhur deer along the road. The trail is nice, but there are quite a few people hiking. Little World's End is the first stop, and World's End is a km or so further. The view from World's End, with its 1000 meter sheer drop, is spectacular in the morning, Before the clouds gather. On the way back, you can stop at Baker's Falls which is a nice place to cool down in some waterfall mist. We heard purple-faced leaf monkeys, but we could not see them. There are plenty of birds around, which are clearly visible in the open moorlands (bring binoculars). Horton Plains is at an altitutde of 2000m (6600 ft), so it can get chilly in the morning. Dress accordingly. As the sun rises, however, it gets hot very quickly.

Tremendous experience and a wonderful hike; the best time to explore is early in the morning just as sun rises. If based in Nuwara'eliya commence the drive to Horton Plains at 5.00AM with a with to reaching the entrance gate at 5.45AM. Tickets can be obtained at the gate (LKR 4,000 foreigners & LKR 60 local). There is usually a tremedous rush to where the hike begins; suggest taking the approximately two kilometre drive slowly taking the opportunity to photograph the mountain range with cloud covers, the white ice covered savannah grass& the surrounding area including the sun rise! The hike: - 2.5 - 4.0 hours depending on the pace, the route is a loop but suggests taking the Devon waterfall end first as the scenery is great for photography during the early morning sunlight - take ample water as there are limited water resources - wear properly covered shoes with good grip as this will enable to go off the track where it is fasinating - distance 8KM on some uneven terrain, but not challenging physically - there is a potential to see great wildlife including the Sri Lankan Leopard - the three key sites are Devon waterfall, World's End and Mini-World's End but the surrounding area is surreal! - Must take: a good camera & a video recording device; if you are DSLR fan take the standard (24-70mm), the wide angle (10-22mm) and a zoom lense with a tripod (Gorillapod) Suggest lagging & avoiding the large groups and taking at your own place to enjoy the surrounding. There is a 'canteen' to purchase some food & water either at the start or end of the hike. Getting there - can be arranged through the hotels or a travel agent or catch a tuk-tuk from the nearest station (Pattipola). There is a marked price difference if organised via the hotel which is US$75-100 per person all inclusive or contact a reliable agent (Kritharan Suresh +94 766 802 892, dedicated vehicle for US$30 plus entrance which could be US$30). P.S - surprised that the locals visit the reserve around 11am when the rest finishes; not sure what the rational is, as it could be quite hot!!

We did this hike half way through our World Challenge expedition with 14 students. After a ridiculously early morning start, we reached the 'top of the world' as the sun rose and it was truly breathtaking. The hike itself has a few areas which are pretty tough but you can avoid the majority of these. The views are stunning and if you're lucky you'll see quite a few wonderful species. The drive up to the park was treacherously twisty so if you get car sick, plan for this!

We arrived at 7:30 on a Saturday and finished the loop by 11:30. In hindsight, I would have arrived about 30 minutes earlier to avoid the incoming crowds on the last bit of the hike. After 11, there were groups of 10+ people carrying crates with food and musical instruments to spend the day. We recommend going to World’s End first, then looping through Baker’s Falls. When we arrived, there was maybe 30 minutes before the clouds made the scenery disappear. Some guides were recommending the opposite direction saying it was less strenuous. Not sure the rationale, since it’s a loop anyways, and we would have missed the views. Some guides were feeding animals (shame!), but the park does a fantastic job at keeping plastic and styrofoam away. Ask your hotel for a packed breakfast in a paper bag. Unfortunately, the park does not turn away loud tourists. Many people are there to get in touch with nature, hear the sounds of the streams and birds. Really not the place to share your thoughts on the volatility of bitcoin or tell everyone how you really feel about Susan. Guides are not required and I didn’t feel are needed — the trail is easy to follow. Bring the longest lenses you have for your camera, and a tripod, if you’re into photography. Some really nice shots to be taken.

We hired a mini van and set off from our hotel at 5am in Nuwara Eliya to avoid queuing as this is the busy season. It was raining i Nuwara Eliya but we took the risk as our driver said it should be dry in Horton Plains. When we got there it was still misty but the mixture of the mist and blue sky made this perfect for the cameras. Advice, try to go early as you can to get the view of the mist as this makes it more beautiful. If you want to get to the mini worlds end and main worlds end quickly as possible then I advise to take the left trail (when the trail splits). However if you go late I suggest take the right as its less busy/touristy, both routes take you to the same places as its circular. Overall really enjoyed it as its medium hiking but its quite expensive (entrance 3500 per person excluding vehicle hire).

Yes, price for tourists is crazy and we didn't really see lots of conservation for the money. Only saw park rangers checking tickets and plastic. More interpretation and an updated visitor centre to get out from the 1980's would be great. The hike was ok but lots of hikers/tourists but this was peak time. Plenty of great orchids and other stuff to see. A bit wet and slippery in places - I would recommend shoes with grip. However, we saw some very interesting examples of footwear that made it through. We did see the Samba deer hanging out around the visitor centre - we only really heard them calling on the walk. We saw monkeys in the trees below from Little Worlds End. We did see a family of Baboon Monkeys (not sure real name) just off the path on the way back after Little Worlds End which was good (we went anti-clockwise). Overall, the view was pretty bloody good and worth the money even though we left early in the crazy rush to get the view without clouds/mist.

Most fresh air we can have there. The samba deer is very friendly with visitors. But government service is very poor but they add the service charge to tickets. The tickets prices for foreign people too expensive but poor service. We have to stay long time in ticketing q the tickets issuing very slowly. They have 2 counters but always open only one.

The drive to Horton Plains is crazy. Very windy roads up the mountain which is not meant for two way traffic. We went very early to avoid the crowds, but I think everyone had the same idea. The queues were long to get into the park.  The walk is 10km (Approx 3 hours) long and it is up and down rocky and sometimes slippery paths but the views and waterfall are worth all of the effort.  We only saw a deer and a few birds, so not much wildlife. The drive back down the mountain was worse as there was traffic both ways on the inadequate roads. It was an enjoyable day out.

But the falls, and the World’s End views are really beautiful.  It’s a moderate hike with some climbing, rocks, mud, etc.  but not too difficult.  Definitely worth 3-4 hours of your time.

It’s a trek of medium difficulty - not so much the elevation differences that you yo-yo through, but rather, the uneven and somewhat un-walkable terrain. Made all the more dreary by the absence of good views as you trundle through, or even at the so-called viewing points like the “End of the World”. It mists up badly as the morning matures, so I suppose you have to start the trek by 7:00 am to catch that. It takes a full 3 hours to cover the 9 km loop. You are better off moving clockwise from the fork as you enter the track. That way you can leg the more difficult half before your lactic acid builds up. And do the flatter walk - and let the water sprinkles at Bakers Fall cool your face - as the home stretch. Wear outdoor boots with rugged, gripping soles. You may encounter a lot of mud - red, brown, black. Pack some paper towel rolls, water (the only plastic they will allow) and basic first aid. Because they have no help anywhere on the track. Which brings to my basic grouch. You spend a packet - first the exorbitant cab fare, then the entrance fees (LKR 3400 per foreign visitor, once you add all the taxes and “service charge” for getting absolutely no service) - and wonder why they can’t spend some of that revenue to improve the condition of the approach road, have some decent sit-n-relax space at the visitor centre, give people at least a map marking the highlights, have a few first aid and water kiosks inside, and invest in posting much required signage along the route. GPRS doesn’t work. You come to a fork and cannot readily figure out which way to go unless you see some people ahead - who may have taken the wrong turn as well! They have these silly information tablets placed at random, talking about fire, trees and soil. These tablets should instead show a map, tell you where you are, and give an idea of which way to go. If you are still all charged up for Horton Plains, go duly equipped and don’t lug heavy photography gear (like I did!). Happy walking and tripping over sundry tree trunks and black mud!

But the scenery around Mahaeliya was fantastic with the Sambar deer appearing out of the thick mist & we enjoyed it very much.. World's end trail area did not get the heavy mist & was sunny with a few drizzles & had a good view at World's end. Baker's falls was in full flow & beautiful but the path was getting crowded. In contrast along the Thotupola trail, it was beautiful & serene with so many wild flowers. The information center is good but can improve & the Wildlife department staff there were helpful. All in all a beautiful experience of nature & we wish to make it again.

We had a 5.30am start to reach the reserve early and the sunrise views, as we ascended the track were undoubtedly stunning. On arrival we waited for our turn to enter. In recent years this has become a general tourist attraction and there are now a lot of vehicles. Consequently, with more disturbance on the walks, it has become less good for birding. It was still possible to see some species and often rather a lot of them, but other forest dwellers are rarely seen. The only animals seen were Sambar deer, now very tame, browsing around the carpark. The price differentials between foreigners and local people have been detailed in other posts. It is understandable that we affluent  visitors pay more than locals who may not be able to afford to travel abroad - but in the case of this national park it was not really worth the expense.

If you book make sure you go prepared...i didn't. You need to layer up as its cold to start out but you'll soon start to heat up. Hiking World's End was something I was looking forward to while in Sri Lanka however, it seems that capturing a good view really depends on the weather for that day. It can easily be a cloudy day in which you really would not see the end of the world. I don't mean to be pessimistic but it really didn't look like the end of the world. (Maybe my expectations were too high). Other than that, the hike is wonderful. You cross a lot of different scenery and walkways. Each side of the hike is different from the other. Upon entering the hiking area, you are not allowed to take anything plastic with you. The guides will take all plastic items away and remove anything that could potentially be dumped as trash. The trails are very well kept and there is hardly any trash on the ground. Note that the drive to the entrance from the main town is very curvy and very likely you will be car sick! Tips: - Wear proper shoes and clothing. It can be very hot and about half of the trail is not shaded and under the sun. - Have your guide drive you to the entrance. If he insists that you need a special jeep don't listen. All the normal tour vans made it up to the top just fine. - Leave early from your hotel. The entrance line can be quite long and getting there early is helpful to beat the crowd. - Make sure to stop by Baker's Fall.

World's End is located in Horton Plain National Park. You'll need to walk a few kilometres before reaching it. There is a 11-km loop that you can take. For that, you'll need proper shoes, as there are some short steep climbs in certain spots. Layer your clothes so you can strip layers before you sweat too much. Get there early, and be prepared to face many other people who want to see the same views (the park opens at 6 am). You may bring bottles into the park, but your bags will be checked thoroughly, so you will have to remove plastic wraps around the bottle and wrap your sandwiches in paper. Paradoxically, I still saw some people bring their breakfast in Styrofoam boxes. These were littering the place after, unfortunately.

World's end is a steep precipices at the edge of Horton plains the world heritage site. To have a clear view it would be best to reach the view point by 9am. It takes about 1 to 11 1/2 hours to reach the small world's end and to proceed to the peak view point. If you are lucky , the view will be clear of mist as ocaasional mist clouds cover the view from time to time. After vieving you should not miss waling up to Baker's water fall on your return erndy whihc is high with bio diversity. If you are a great treker of mountains, you are free to climb the second highest mountain of the island" Kirigalpoththa" but not on the same day as this also would take about 4 hours. It may be noted that no plastics, o bottles or lunch parcels are permitted . Therfore you should carry your water in a permanent bottle. and all snacks in paper bags. Be ready to face cold weather as the weather or the climate rapidly changes. enjoy the train jerney from Kandy to Ohiya, stay the night in Ohiya and start  a jerney of 10 km from Ohiya to Hortain plains as early as possible so that you can be their by sun rise. Arrange your mode of transport from Ohiya the previous evening. A tuk-tuk or a safari jeep will do the job for you . DON'T fail to carry your water and snacks from Ohiya as no boutiques or shops will be available within the 10km  between Ohiya and Hortan plains.

It really feels like the world has ended here. Amazing view from here, I believe this is a must visit in Nuwara Eliya. At Horton Plains, there are mainly three tourist spots, World's end, mini World's end and Baker's Fall. I would recommend to reach there in the morning as early as possible as clouds come by and blocks the view later.

Make sure you arrive at Horton Plains as early as possible as the walk can get hot and uncomfortable as the day progresses. Wear a hat and protect your neck/back (if you have short or bunned-up hair) - I ended up with a sun-burnt back as much of the walk is on the open plains with no shade. Under the unforgiving sun and heat, the 11km walk can seem unending. Worth a visit nonetheless. Be prepared with water and food.

This has been on the bucket list for some time. Wasn't disappointed. We took the clockwise route to WE, leaving the car park at 7:45am. Took about 45min to get there and luckily not too busy. Great views when you get there but it's not just about the view. There are many different flora and fauna treats not to mention the passing parade of friendly chirpy fellow visitors. Among others, we came across a colourful beetle and a green lizard on our walk as we continued clockwise past Bakers Fall back to the start, exhausted but exhilarated. One of the things I love about Sri Lanka is their attention/commitment to preserving our environment. Well done. This national park is testament to that - our driver/guide advised us that no plastic was permitted to be taken into the park. We had to remove all plastic labels from our water bottles and on the 10km walk there was no sign of any environmentally unfriendly litter. Incredible in this day and age.

We got up at 430am to drive from Nuwara Eliya here hoping to beat the crowds and catch the morning light. Unfortunately this idea is published in every guidebook so everyone else also had this idea. After a queue to get tickets we traipsed in a long line to get to the viewing platforms. If you go up the cliff between worlds end and little worlds end it's quieter and a better view than the 'official' platforms filled with people taking selfies. Views are great if you can avoid the urge to boot the selfie takers off of the edge. The park is well run though and the approach to litter is great. Overall a nice walk but we had better (quieter) ones during our stay in Sri Lanka.

If you like hiking and aren't afraid to put in the effort for about 10km, then this hike is definitely one of Sri Lanka if not the worlds best. Make sure to set off early enough in the morning and you'll get to see the sunrise before you start plus it won't be so hot as you're finishing later. The trek is well maintained and kept clean, there's only a few bins around so you'll need to carry your empty water bottles either to those bins or back out with you. We walked in the direction of Little Worlds End, Worlds End and then Bakers Fall.  The waterfall was worth seeing, not huge but relaxing to sit in the shade and cool breeze from the water. Definitely glad I was able to do this trek as the views are amongst the best of my trip.

We left Nuwara Elija a bit before 5am and reached the park entrance before the ticket counter opened at 6am. There was already a queue waiting at the ticket office- so better be early. In the park, I would recommend hiking 'left' or 'clockwise' to reach mini worlds end and worlds end faster. Also, this part of the hike is mainly in the shady forest whereas the route via the waterfalls leads through the open plains. For the whole tour we needed approx. 2.5h. Thanks to our early arrival and 'clockwise' hike we reached worlds before the other tourists and could enjoy the two worlds ends all to ourselfs. Be prepared: in August at 5-7 am you require long trousers and a jacket-it's freezing. As soon as the sun is out for a while however, temperatures rise very fast and you need proper sun protection- it's burning hot. Bring a large bottle of water and wear good shoes. We saw people in flipflops, without sunhat or water start for the tour in the late morning... I wouldn't recommend that. To sum up: be early, be prepared and you'll have a great morning hike.

Avoid this tourist trail at all costs. We got up at 4.30am to get to worlds end early but there were already at least 50 minivans in the car park disgorging their tourist hordes. The trail is beautiful but you never get away from people and there is no sense of getting away from it all. Our walks in Ella were far more spectacular and free and without the trail of tourists in front and behind.

The drive here is quite long from Nuwara Eilya with windy roads. The walk is 9km with some short bursts of hills. Allow three hours if you walk at a decent pace which allows for photos stops, a food break and seeing Bakers falls. Weather can change quickly here and we were surprised at the unsuitable clothing and footwear being worn by some. A pair of trainers is a good idea and an umbrella in case of a shower. The advice we had to go early was also good as mist comes in and stops the view. Our guide was able to take us on a small, not much used path for a wonderful view of the viewing platform itself and the World End view. This was better than the real thing as we could appreciate the sheer drop and we were on our own. The actual area was quite busy with lots of people jostling for photos. Not great at the edge of a sheer drop!! Anyone with vertigo or young children may wish to stand back!!

Worlds end is a great view, but it is more the getting there that is the highlight. The high plains filled with miniature bamboo, rhododendrons and patches cloud forest are great to walk through. Worlds end is a good drop off with a view of the villages far below. Lots of other people walking on trail, so be prepared for people traffic on the trail.

The Worlds End hype is rather very blown out of proportion. Its a very long walk ( about 9 km in all ) to go see a view point that is rather ok if not disappointing . Lets be honest im not the fittest of characters and nor is trekking and outdoors my fancy , so probably i didnt enjoy it too much , but the trek can get really tiring especially if you have kids on board.

9 + km hike early morning was interesting. From worlds end it's 2 contrast walks. Water fall on the way back was very soothing. Never seen that many "Rhododendron" plants in my life and all blooming with red flowers.Only advice is commence your walk as early as possible.

Absolutely great place to see and a good hiking to do in the Horton plains. Thought the entry to the park is quite expensive for tourists. If you are luckey the fog dissapears and you can have a beautiful view at World's End and Mini World's End. But honestly, it is a long hike for just to viewingplaces.

World's End is a gem! While a bit on the pricey side, and with quite a wait to get in even at 6 a.m., the beautiful hike and the gorgeous views more than made up for it. We loved the trail from Little World's End to World's End - not the one most ppl take, but the one going straight up and then mostly along the edge of the mountain. Three hours might be a good time to spend here, but I could have stayed the whole day, just the same. Do take note, though, that the recommendation to come early - which you will find in just about all the guidebooks - is a good one. We got up at 4:30 a.m., and it was well worth it.

We are a retired couple who did the 9.5 km walk. We took our time as the walk is not easy. There are lots of rocks and steep climbs as well as the walk along the plains. I had been here about 15 years prior and was quite surprised to see how much development had taken place, yet how the scenery still remained the same. it'll always be one of my favourite places to visit and this time was no exception, even being 6 months pregnant. The views are breathtaking and the entire area is just gorgeous.

World's End is a sheer precipice located at the southern boundary of the Horton Plains National Park. Access is from the Horton Plains visitors centre from where we walked on foot for about 5 km. There were clear directions and the difficulty level would be moderate. The view from the World's End is beautiful and the best time to visit is early morning, say around 8 am.

We woke up at 5am to catch the sunrise from World's End. The entire Horton's Plain trek is about an 8km loop. Give yourself 2.5-3 hours for this. Wear comfortable shoes and bring a thick pullover. The winds can get pretty rough. The hike is of moderate intensity and most people should be able to make it. If you are pressed for time, it's a 3km hike in to World's End. Retrace your route out and you'll be done in 6km.

This was really the saviour to our trip to Nuwara Eliya, which was incredibly misty and cold as it was off season. The walk was lovely and the views spectacular! Baker's falls are also beautiful. The hike to the actual 'worlds end' point took an hour or so. Relatively easy and short compared to climbing Adams Peak! Trekking to World's End is understandably rated as one of the best things to do in Nuwara Eliya. It is strongly recommended, but proper planning is required to have full enjoyment of the experience. First of all, don't be discouraged by reviewers who report that the trek is so difficult and strenuous.  This is NOT a hugely strenuous hike; anyone in moderately good fitness can easily make this trek.  The total distance is reportedly about 12 kilometers total, but it seems it might be a little less. The loop distance is a bit over 7 kilometers, plus another few kilometers from the check-in point and back.  The trails are very well maintained and mostly of gentle slope (with just a few portions that are a bit steep). A few things to consider in planning your hike: - important to know the price in advance; the fee is a little over 3,000 rupees per person (my wife and I paid 6,500 for the two of us, plus the fee for local driver and the sizable service charge) - from Nuwara Eliya, hikers have to travel som 25 kilometers to the start of the trek; this will take 45 minutes to an hour - the access road is very steep in places; while cars can make the steep grades OK, the road sometimes backs up with full-sized buses trying to make the trip with great difficulty (best to go early enough to avoid the buses) - tickets are purchased at a ticket sales office some 5 kilometers from the start of the hike - about 1.5 km into the hike is a fork; the right path is more exposed, so if it's a hot day, you may wish to go that direction first; that way, you'll be hiking more in the shade during the final stretch on the return - the entire loop hike will take most people about 3 to 4 hours; my wife and I are in our late 50s and early 60s so we took our time and made several stops along the way and still finished the entire hike in about 4 hours - some who more fit, or in a hurry, do the entire hike in as little as 2.5 hours - the views at the World's End lookout and at the Mini World's End (not really so "mini") are superb; sometimes shrouded in fog and clouds, but wait for them to clear and enjoy the spectacular views Don't be discouraged and don't miss this wonderful hike!

Highly recommend this walk! The best one we did in Sri Lanka! Beautiful scenery and accommodates to most people with a basic level of fitness. A number of view points on the way (Mini World End, Worlds End and some waterfalls etc.), which lead to a consistently nice sites and views. Make sure to get there early (6.30am) as it gets very busy with other walkers/drivers at the entrance all trying to buy tickets. We lucked out and I guess it's pot luck as to do the walk in fog would be a completely wasted effort. First up, I was fully prepared for the long walk on an undulating terrain - had professional hiking shoes, ample packed breakfast and bottles of water, cap, sun-block, rain gear, etc. I am also used to hiking on far more difficult terrains. Consequently, I was able to finish the entire round-trip in 2.5 hours flat. I started my hike from the ticket check-point at a little before 7.00 AM - which was the right thing to do because as I was completing my trip the mist had already draped much of the area. Coming to the place, well, the sights are nothing to crow about. Such hikes are dime a dozen back here in India and around the world. The sights at the World's End of the valley, far away water bodies and mountains are good and a photographer's delight. But remember, price is what you pay, value is what you get. For an entry fee of LKR 3,842 I wouldn't recommend this hike to anybody. Suggestions for those who would still be interested in the hike: 1) Make sure you commence your hike by 7:00 AM. When you reach a fork, take the path on the left which takes you to the World's End first. The reason for doing so is to beat the mist and have ample time to savour the sights. There is also a long queue at the ticket counter - budget half an hour for it. 2) Carry rain jackets 3) Wear a good pair of hiking shoes 4) Your hotel would probably supply you packed breakfast. Make sure you don't carry it in plastic bags or boxes. They are confiscated at the entry checkpoint. 5) Don't feed the wild animals, if you encounter any. It corrupts their natural foraging abilities. 6) The hike isn't difficult for 95% of the walk. The balance 5% is moderate uphill climb. Again, not difficult, but older people might find it convenient to carry walking poles.

There are two three options if you really crazy about hiking. By road, you can walk or go by vehicle. GO EARLY (meaning reach at 6am) - the queue starts building up and our driver mentioned that there are only a few hours of no fog after sunrise. If you plan to do this, bring a WINDPROOF jackets as the wind is superstrong at the ticketing area and it is very cold in the morning. Better still, have two layers of jacket, the other one being a warm jacket with fillings. We were illprepared and caught a cold which was not pleasant for the rest of our trip. The ticket price for us was 6150LKR - which is for 2 adults + 1 car. You would do well with only the windproof jacket afterwards, as there are some areas of the walk which are relatively open and hence still windy. The other jacket is not needed (leave it in the car?), as you will tend to heat up and sweat whilst hiking. The starting area is some distance away from the ticketing area, and we saw an elk along the way (which you can feed bananas for some great photos). Otherwise, the drive to the starting area was foggy but cleared up quickly once we reached the starting area. At the starting area, you will be subjected to a bag check and all form of plastic will be removed and thrown away. The route is a circular route and so you can choose left / right. We picked the left route (Mini Worlds End > Worlds End > Bakers Fall). The hike is intermediate, with the need to climb up and down tree roots and rocks - jeans and sports shoes recommended (no slippers / heels please). The plains area (but windy so the jacket is good here) is just shrubbery and devoid of life, and the forested area is, well, forest (and no wind). The attraction points are BEAUTIFUL though - no railings at the edge so watch yourself. Baker's Fall is well worth the hundred steep steps up and down (even though it is the last attraction and you will likely be sporting tired legs). Overall it was a good but lengthy hike.

You must really love hiking to do Horton plains up to World's End. It is a long hike and a strenous one at time. Broken pathways mean climbing over rocks and boulders. I thoroughly loved this and would do it again! Thw views arw amazing and Baker's falls is mesmerizing. Be sure to carry lots of water and have an average of 3 hours to spare.

First of all, it's best to arrive at 6am when the ticket office opens, to avoid the crowds of tourists and locals alike. So after very little sleep and an hours drive up winding roads (feeling very travel sick) we arrived at worlds end. Now this is a cloud forest, so expect cool temperatures and clouds... The only thing was, we didn't anticipate quite so much cloud... We couldn't see anything! There was no view visible at all from mini worlds end and only a partial view for about 10 minutes when cloud cleared slightly at the main worlds end viewpoint. The rest of the walk through the site was picturesque and the steep bank down to the waterfalls is worth it. We saw Samba and enjoyed our trip overall (it was an adventure after all) but for 4000 rupees I believe you're better off visiting in a different season- not August!

We got up at 4.30am and drove about an hour to worlds end we were tired but it was worth it. If you walk left first at the Y bend its mostly downhill and rocky (i would want to climb up it after 10km) at the end if you walk left its mainly sandy and easy walking with great views. Also if you walk left 1st your not fighting with locals entering at 9am whe you are returning. Great views, great waterfall, sore feet but worth the wake up and walk. Take sensible shoes/trainers And for the morning an extra jumper/hoodie by the end you may not need it. I wish i bought my ear warmers as its very windy at some of the views....but my ears get so cold anyway. Enjoy!

We didn't fancy getting up at 5am to get up here for the walk, so we opted for the much less onerous excursion of a drive up this mountainous road to the entrance to the Park itself. OK, it was a bit of a cop out, but the walk is a fairly arduous 9km, at height, and my husband felt it would be too much for him. However, thanks to an experienced and knowledgeable local guide/driver, we had a hugely enjoyable morning. The terrain changes constantly as the road rises, and the morning mists make it all extremely atmospheric. Our guide pointed out lots of plants, animals and birds, and stopped all the time for photos. We spent some time at the highest station in Sri Lanka (my husband loves old trains). Really interesting trip - but be warned, if you want to walk to The World's End, it can be very cold, wet, slippy - and a really early start. If you're up to it, I'm sure it would be immensely rewarding though.

World's End is a spot on the trek of Horton plains national park. The spot is famous for its 800 m vertical drop. The entry to Horton plains national park is around LKR-3000/- for foreigners. Best time to go is early morning so you can see the sunrise. It is better to hire a jeep from city to Horton Plains (you should book it a night before). Jeeps normally take around LKR-4000 for a round trip from the city center to Horton plains and back. Total hike is around 9kms and you need to be fit to complete it. It normally takes around 3.5 hours to complete the trek.

The view from World's End is absolutely stunning! Go early so you can see the view (apparently its shrouded in fog by around 10am) and dress in many layers! It was freezing at 5.30am but I ended getting sunburned in the heat of the late morning. Also avoid bringing plastic bags as there's a checkpoint where they'll take them from you to avoid litter in the park.

We visited World's End when it was raining and the fog had left no visibility. The drive to the world's end is complicated with lots of twists and turns, so go with an experienced driver. As we reached the entrance, it was crazy cold, you couldn't see anything due to the fog and we were contemplating whether to pay the steep entrance fee or not. But we're glad we made the decision to go anyway. And you should too. No matter what, just go in! You can drive 5 kms into the plains and then you have to park and walk ahead. You have small eateries here so best to grab a bit before you set off. A cup of noodles or Rotty would be good. The walk itself is easy and offers great views. The fog situation keeps changing so keep walking. There is no need for a guide as you can follow signs and reach the points. On your way, you can see Baker's Falls, Mini World's End and World's End - each comes with its own charm. Walk at your speed, stop and marvel and this vast expanse of gorgeousness. Spend a whole day just walking around if you can.

we were lucky to start our trip early morning as we didn't feel much tired even after the long walk. We started around 6am and we could come to the end by 10.30am. Also we were able to see the beautiful sceneries since there was no sun. Really enjoyed

Fabulous national park, but be aware that even if you arrive at 6am, there will be queues and despite the huge area, it is difficult to escape the other visitors on the single circular path. The Chinese visitors had wrapped using hotel bathrobes. Enterprising.

The following might be a bit lengthy but I want to describe this with some detail to give a good idea of my experience, so bear with me. We were told by our main driver that we needed to get a 'jeep' to take us to Horton Plains, which would cost $50 (7200 LKR). Having read some reviews on trip advisor I knew that this trip could be made with 3500-5000LKR. When I told this to our driver he laughed and said 'They will tell you they're coming with a jeep but they come with a small car'. He also said that the jeep driver would queue in the cold to get our tickets and we would stay in the car while he did so. We did not make a fuss. The next morning a driver arrived at 5am, not with a jeep as promised, but with a big van that could fit about 8 people (what a waste of space and fuel). It was a 1 hour drive from our hotel in Nuwara Eliya up a steep and winding road. When we got to the top the van driver told us to go and buy our tickets (3200 LKR each). Fortunately when we argued that we were told otherwise he went and got them for us. At the top there were a lot of normal cars and even tuk tuks which made us feel like we had been deceived into believing we required a 'jeep' for this journey. The hike itself was good but unfortunately we did not get to see much of World's End as it had been raining the previous days and there was a lot of mist. I am sure that if it had been a clear day the view would have been amazing. Baker's Falls is nothing spectacular, only a small waterfall. We though the entry price to the Horton Plains was extremely expensive, considering this is a NATURE trail. There are some toilets on the trail but are in a very bad condition: broken, filthy, no paper and doors that don't close and fling open with the breeze. There is also a cafe at the beginning/end of the trail which is also very uninviting. There is nothing that justifies the 3200 LKR entry pice. Me and my boyfriend both felt ripped off. There are many nature trails in Europe that are equally good and even better and which are free.

I could understand why it called as world's end! I've got refreshed in the magnificent nature!

If you're visiting this part of Sri Lanka then a trip to Horton Plains National Park and World's End is a must.  All the other reviews give the basics but the most important points are: get there early (by 6 am); make sure you have decent walking shoes or good quality trainers, a waterproof and a couple of layers of clothing for warmth; take something to eat and drink (but bags will be inspected and anything likely to harm animals, e.g., plastic labels on bottles will be removed). We went round anti-clockwise, which meant that the steep steps were are the beginning, and downwards, rather than at the end and upwards.  I'm in my early 50s and of ok fitness, and found the walk reasonable but definitely felt tired at the end!  It would be too difficult I think for a 5 year old, but an 8 year old would find it easy. Given the general costs in Sri Lanka, this is an expensive trip...it cost us (2 people) around £60-70 for a car with driver and entrance into the park, but definitely worth it!  The views at World's End were spectacular and we were lucky enough to see the views despite heavy mists and drizzle in the area.

It was busy but still peaceful at the same time sat on the edge of the rock. I would definitely recommend coming here.

This is a nice park to go for a walk and tick the World's End box, plus a small waterfall, but it has a lot of negatives for us. You can get equally impressive views from Ella Rock (and the Buddha nearby) for free with better weather and quieter. We paid 1750slr per person for a van of 6. And approx 3000slr to enter the park. Reasons not to go: 3000slr to enter park. Ella Rock is free, equal views. 5pm rise (tourists go at this hour, locals tend to go later in the day, supposedly better chances of views in the morn) Queues of multiple vans carrying very few people all the way there (little attempt by a lot of accommodation to help you go in a group, but just ask around in town and you'll find a group) Fumes off all the vans in traffic was a problem for us. But to clarify our van driver was very informative and accommodating, (even if he only did our transport) Worst part: you will have to queue for approx an hour and due to the climate there is high probability it will be misty, foggy and windy. We were well prepped with hats, full rain gear and ponchos, but some people were in shorts and sandles and soaked. This is due to one window for everyone, and every group ticket having to be printed on the spot. Very inefficient, unnecessary and no attempt to fix it. Very little wildlife (due to next point). But there are deer that will come close, because unfortunately there are some tourists giving them food so they expect it. Too many people for an average and overcrowded view. We actually got the perfect weather when at the view point but it is simply very crowded. In general, we found a lot of ignorant, and inconsiderate chinese tourists which cause a lot of the issues, such as shouting, feeding the deer, overtaking viewpoints. Note that no matter how bad the weather in the morning, it almost always clears up. To prove this point, our driver said he wouldn't charge us if it didn't clear up.

If you are a couple and want flexibility of when to leave your accomodation and when to leave the National Park afterwards get a Tuk Tuk. Pay no more than 2500-3000R for a return journey with the driver waiting during the 4 hour hike.  The journey takes 1hr 10 mins in a Tuk Tuk. We left at 6:30am (most tour operators using vans leave at 5:30am and then wait in a big queue)...the Tuk Tuk can skirt around these queues on this single track road. We walked in the sunshine although the drive was in the rain. The view was great....but hugely overpriced. See photo for prices of tickets. Locals pay 60R plus taxes!! Tourist pay 2058R plus taxes. A one-off service charge of 1097R will be added to each (tourist/foreigners) group booking...so combining into a bigger group will mean this charge only being paid once and subdivided between the group. Check the weather before you go as it will be a wasted journey if the conditions are not right.

Go early and wrap up warm.  It took us around 25 mins to buy tickets and get through the gate and we had underestimated how cold and misty/wet it would be at 6am. The view from worlds end is great. I can't deny that. If you are going mainly for that take the left hand trail and come back after seeing it, rather than doing the whole loop. The main negative I found was that I wasn't overawed by anything else. The waterfall is nice, but not worth the clambering over roots and things. Maybe I'm just a bit cynical, but the landscape was not that different to the Scottish highlands, the Peak District or even the Surrey Hills, all of which are free to access for everyone. I found the terrain frustrating as you had to clamber roots and rocks, meaning you couldn't enjoy the landscape en route, even if you wanted to. (This isn't a quirk of the landscape but erosion of footfall over time). There's nothing wrong with this but, other than the view, it's just a walk in the park. TIP: if you're traveling alone or in a pair, try to join up with another group to get a group ticket which works out cheaper. As a group of 4 it was 2650 each instead of 3700 for an individual ticket. NOTE: if you have any back, knee, hip or ankle issues take the left trail and come back after worlds end. You DO need a basic level of fitness for this or you'll just not enjoy it.

Be warned! Its a well oiled tourist machine, and a long walk for a nice view. Take the Train from Nuwara Eliya to Ella instead - the views go on for ever and it is a much more enjoyable experience!

The entire walk covering mini-worlds end, worlds end and bakers falls is about 10.5km. Dont get fooled by the distance you end up climbing and going down as well. The whole journey including stops took us about 5 and a 1/2 hours. Its good to have some level of fitness for your own good. On a clear day the view is amazing. By evening the mist starts setting and the feeling and view takes you to another world. If its your day, you will be able to see Elk close to the pathway.  At the end all that you have gone through is fully worth it. This is an experience that is "out of this world"

The walk takes a morning if your walking as a family. Make sure you go early as even arriving at 7 we were still unable to see down off worlds end (although if you walk round via mini worlds end first then you should get to see all you need).

We got up very early to avoid risking to be in the mist and not experiencing the beautiful view. At 6:30 there was a long queue at the ticket office in the cold and misty weather with only one officer issuing the tickets. It took almost an hour before we could really start walking. The traxk and the surroundings are very nice. A good track of 3550 meters to the worlds end and 3550 meters back. Although the ticket office was still in the mist, the real walk was in nice sunny weather. A lot of others did the same walk but it was not too crowded. May be too many selfies? It is also nice to experience the view through your own eyes! All in all very much worth doing this trip but we recommend lowering the ticket price. 20 euro per person for a nice walk is really overpriced.

First: I am not in good shape at all, and was concerned that i could not do the 10km walk. However, i tell you that YES you can do it and don't have to be a hiker or a walker. Just take your time, follow our advice and you too can enjoy a trip to the top of the world. 2nd: give it a pass if it is raining, or rained the previous day unless you like trekking in the mud and scrambling up the slopes. If misty or wet, leave the kids at home. Dry, it is great even for the little ones. 3rd: Take the trail to the right-- Baker Falls first (have your breakfast there) you will have a much more pleasant experience. You will go down hill going down down and for the most part coming back a little up hill but flat. Look at my trail pictures 4th: Go first thing in the morning to avoid the crowds. Take food but avoid the plastic containers as they will take them away 5th: wear shoes, don't need hiking boats but sandals not good idea although you see people wearing them. The view once you get to the top and yes lots of chinese taking selfies' but that is part of our tourist world now. You will get your turn; but the most solitude and best scenery is the walk along the way. Make sure you spend some time at Baker Falls-- that was the best part of the trip

The World's End is situated in Horton's planes. There are a few other notable highlights alongside the road but let's start with the basics. As of July 2016 it cost 2 people 6200sri lankan rupees. We had to take a truck-looking Safari vehicle from Nuwera Eiliya and that has additional cost. However it was much easier than a car or a mini van. Some of them couldn't even climb up to the entrance as the road was quite slippery. We left Nuwera Eiliya at 4:50am and that was definitely a good time. 6am the park opens and by the time we were up most of the fog was cleared out. 600m after the entrance we had a choice - go left and have Poor Man's World's End (Small World's End) -> Word's End -> Baker's waterfall -> Chimney pool or go right and have them the other way around. Eventually we walked all, of course, but it does make slight difference which road one chooses. Overall it is quite an easy hiking, closer even to leisurely walk at some points. We took the right path and that is also the one I recommend as it is more difficult at first and then it gets easier towards the end. It starts with planes and then around a hill corner and into a forest. There you can find the waterfall, worth a stop but also the 40 steps upwards from it are the most "difficult" part of the hike. Afterwards there is a bit more forest, slightly challenging if the ground is wet and an opening to the planes. There is again the choice of left and right - left is the toilet :) Next stop is World's end. There are two plates, don't go only to the first one as the second one is higher, quieter and has a comfortable breakfast spot. Moving forward, about a kilometer further through the woods is poor man's world's end. The views are just as great, trust me! A couple of hundred meters further there are steps to a toilet that has the greatest view I've ever seen form one (carry your own napkins). You will walk uphill on a bit of rocks and then the path opens up in the forest to almost a 2-lane road! It's quite easy to walk this part of the path and don't forget to take a lot of pictures along the way. The complete walk took us 3hrs considering that we had half an hour breakfast break. Some people choose to go only to the small World's end and walk 4km instead of the 9km. Then they would take the left path on the initial fork and have an easy road ahead and then walk back the same route after they've seen the small World's End. If you feel that the big walk is too much for you the small one also offers amazing views. But please keep in mind I've done all my hikes so far in havaiana sandals and this 9km one was no different and not even close to the most challenging :) so give it a shot and see the full thing!

The 9.5km was mostly an easy walk with just a few uphill sections. The views at Mini World's End and World's End are beautiful. Baker's Falls is pretty too. We did start at 7:30 am though so maybe if you go a little earlier it might be quieter? We came to Nuwara Eliya on a very British day, cold (10c), wet and raining. This was weather we didn't even know existed in Sri Lanka off the back of the warmth everywhere else.  Our walk was very misty i.e. in the cloud's which is quiet normal for this area and the wind on the open spaces made it quiet unpleasant. But inspite of all the cold and wet, we really enjoyed the challenging walk. It's for a reasonably fit person as it's 9km of solid walking on natural rock and soil surfaces. And if you come on a day like we did you will need good shoes/trainers/walking boots and a waterproof/windproof jacket. This place is definitely worth a visit if you are near by but if you don't come dress appropriately you will not enjoy it. We didn't see much wildlife on the walk but the flat field's from the entrance and the registration building were full of deer who were very comfortable with a small moving and quiet human presence. If we were to go again and the weather was bad I think we would just do Little World's End as this is only a 5km round trip. The view is very similar to World's end and I think you wouldn't be constantly wishing to be back in Warm Sunny Sri Lanka. We saw a girl in flip flops, jeans and just a shirt at the first stop and she was insistent on not seeing the next site and just turning back. Many Chinese and Japanese came fashionably dressed with umbrella's but the open fields will break even the strongest umbrella. Being incorrectly dressed will also slow your walk down. Ensure you take enough water and an early start is suggested, incase it's a clear day, as the heat will get to you on such a long walk. Park entry was approx 3000RS per person plus you have to pay for your guide and car at a small cost of around 300RS

We booked a tuk tuk through our guesthouse in Nuwara Eliyah for 3500 rupees. We were picked up at 5am in order to do a morning walk. Views off both small world's end and the world's end are stunning.  Also a little bit scary because they really are sheer drops! We did the whole 9km loop and the whole walk was beautiful,  ranging from plains to forest and waterfall walks. We seen deer,  monkeys and some funky looking lizards.  The walk was not too difficult,  but also not as easy as some of the guide books seem to suggest. I would say it was a moderate walk. It is not too steep,  but there are lots of boulders to walk over. Someone elderly or with bad joints may find this more difficult. It could be quite slippery,  so I would imagine it would be a lot more difficult in the rain. There was a cafe and toilet facilities at the beginning of the walk and a couple of stops along the way.
