For the people who are visiting Nuwara Eliya , World'End is the main attraction. First thing first The travelers who need to explore World'End need to start the journey latest by 0530 in the morning from Nuwara Eliya. This is to facilitate you complete your approx 18 km (09 km one way) walk by 1030 am before the sunlight gets directly above you and to get better view without mist falling down. Suggest to take packed breakfast as you can have it during the drive from Nuwaraeliya. The drives takes approximately an hour. The road signs are hardly visible but I managed to do with google maps. If you are carrying online version, the cellular data is almost getting lost close to Horton Plains and be mindful about it. If you are suffering from any injury or not 100% fit please avoid as there is no medical facility or first aid to be seen after you leave Nuwara Eliya. If not you got to be self sufficient with your first aid kit. As there is no cellular coverage or emergency medical services , there is no way you could get anyone for assistance unless you get hold of someone who is doing the same excursion to help you. Please be mindful about it and try to be self sufficient for the journey. My advice is not to take tuk tuk from Nuwara Eliya as the hilly terrain doesn't give you the best safety in a tuk tuk . As I have explained you can reach the ticket counter at 0630 am, if you leave Nuwara Eliya by 0530 am. You need to buy your tickets from the counter located at the left side and then move to the opposite ( right side of the road) counter to get your tickets registered. The drive from the ticket counter to Horton Plains is about 10 minutes. If you arrive early you have the opportunity to get a premium parking slot for your vehicle close to start point of the excursion. You really need to take only the essentials as you might end up exhausted at the middle of the walk. Walking shoes is a must and you will not be comfortable at all with sandals or slippers with the uneven rough terrain. There is a check point at the stat point where they check and register your ticket once again and check your bags for any polytene or plastic items which you might leave behind and come. I was allowed to take my water bottle but the seal was removed by them. There is an area where you got to walk under a thick canopy of trees which I found most difficult terrain during entire walk. This note is made especially for the travelers to get prepared themselves to have a smoother trouble free excursion.

Worlds end, mini worlds end and Baker falls are all on the Horton plains walk - around 10 Km. a nice walk but it take a while to get up to the plains (at 7,400 Ft) and there can be delays at entry as only one person works in teh ticket hut which is a bit strange when you see the number of vans waiting. We arrived by 8.30 a.m. to complete the walk before the midday heat caused the clouds to rise and obscure the view. Although the car park was heaving with coaches and minibuses we barely saw 50 people until the last half hour - and spread over 7 km and 3 hours that's really not a lot. At the entrance (the price is a bit steep, but if you're early you get fantastic views before the clouds come) you get your bag checked and any excess packaging or plastic is confiscated. You're allowed water bottles (take off any protective film and labels) and we had two packs of cookies which they permitted as long as we didn't leave the wrappers in the park. The first part of the path is the worst - there's a gentle upward slope of about 200 metres which has been cobbled in a nightmarish way - if ever you were going to break an ankle it's here. Once you've successfully negotiated that helltrap, the rest of the walk is not difficult. After a few hundred metres you reach the loop where you can head left to the viewpoints first, or right to the waterfall first. If you're early always go to the viewpoints first. The first few kilometres are fairly easy, although some of the path consists of big rocks to clamber over. You reach Little World's End after about 2.5km - a stunning viewpoint and a great place to pause for a while. About 1.5km further on is the main World's End - incredible views with a nice firm platform to enable the more nervous to get close to the edge without too much worry. You can scramble up the hill if you wish but there's no real need, the views are astounding anyway. I'd guess this point is just short of the halfway mark. You then head off across the plains towards Baker's Falls. There are a few sections here that are a bit tough, the path climbs steeply up through woodland, so while there are 'steps' some of them consist of enormous tree roots or massive boulders. After about 2.5km more you reach the waterfalls. The path to the actual falls deviates off the main path and down about 50 steps, which obviously you have to climb back up again afterwards! But the falls are worth seeing, plus it's lovely and cool down there - the best place for lunch! After the falls it's a fairly easy 2 km or so back to the car park. By the time we reached this part it was approaching midday and we met quite a lot of locals heading in the opposite direction - some with pushchairs which is something I certainly wouldn't have attempted. If you're worried about whether you can do this walk, bear in mind I'm over 40, 22 stone, unfit, asthmatic and have a very dodgy ankle. I took it steady and really did not find it hard at all, apart from a couple of short sections.

This is my second trip to world and with a Chinese family my role was as a tour guide. I recommend people who wish to walk to world's end to take the right side to enter and left side to exit. It will make you not to feel tiered much when you way back after seen world's end.

The trek to Worlds End is well worth doing. The cool highlands are a beautiful contrast to tropical heat of the lowlands. As others have commented there was little in the way of wildlife, but the scenery more than makes up for it. Just don't expect any solitude as everyone rushes round to see the view in the morning before it clouds over. Which brings me to the downsides. The section of the path to Worlds End is pretty good, but coming back via Baker's falls the going is very rough in places and there are some big steps up and down where the path has washed away. So I would say  effort for the walk is medium, difficulty is hard and if you are not good over rough terrain you should consider skipping the falls and retracing your steps from WE. You also have to expect a queue to get in (30mins+) and no USABLE toilet facilities in the park. Come on SL you are collecting a lot in fees, the least you should be providing is clean toilet facilities near WE and you should repair the path. I suspect that some of the guide books that say the trek is easy are based on how it was when the paths were first made up. They need constant repair and I guess some input from people who know how to make paths through this kind of terrain and climate would help!

We really enjoyed World's End.  It isn't a particularly strenuous hike, but you should have better shoes than mine, as the gravel or dirt can be slippery in places.  I think the whole loop took us about three hours.  We didn't bring food along, but wished we had, as there are some nice spots for a little picnic.  Also don't forget sunscreen--lots of people came out of Horton Plains with bad burns!

Getting their early is a must. We started from Nuwara Eliya at 5.30u On our way we could see the sunrise. The nature itself is most amazing. I would suggest taking your time visiting the park, rather than rush trough it not to miss your train (to Ella). We took the 13.30u train to Ella rather than the 10.15 one.

Amazing hike in the park and views at World's End. We got to World's End about 8:30 and the clouds started rolling in at about 8:50 so definitely hussle to get there. We did the path that went to Mini World's End first and I think that it is the way to go, it is flat and should be faster (make a left by the sign after the visitor center). Also, you cannot have plastic bags, like shopping plastic bags from the grocery store but ziplock bags are okay.

A unique and strange piece of nature. I enjoyed every step towards and from the highlights. We drove in from Nuwara Eliya very early, on our way to Ella. We didn't rush into things and took our time to get fascinated. Suggest to take the 13.30u train to Ella, rather than the 10.20u.

Overall I loved the trek through Horton Plains. The Word's Ends offers a breathtaking view. It is though, a very expensive view, as we can find similar scenarios or better for free and we don't have to queue for 1h+ at 6am in the morning to get the ticket to get in the park.

Honestly I have never been such a place.It was 4 km waking distance at the Horton Plain Nation Park.It is really worth to see and you can see the bottom very clearly if you lucky.I kept my shutter busy to collect some amazing pictures here. Highly recommended to visit this amazing place.

We rented a mini van to get up to the park (Cost 4500 rupees), they pick you up from your hotel around 5am. When you get up to the top, you will need to pick up your tickets to enter the park, the time we went there was a massive rush as there's so many people going. By the time we parked at the park entrance it's about 7am. They check your bags before letting you inside as they don't want you to bring in stuff which could harm the wildlife (like plastic bags or wrappers on bottles). We had to eat some of the food we brought with us before entering. FYI would recommend bringing water and sandwiches or something as the trek itself takes about 4hrs and you cannot buy food there that early. The trek itself was nice, the paths are uneven so wear suitable clothing and footwear. At some point during the trek, you will either to decide which direction you want to go (it's a big circle so you'll see everything either way you pick). I took the left path to the "mini" world's end first. But if I did it again I would go right to the waterfall first. I feel the path was very difficult to come back, especially around the waterfall around in the trees where the path is steep. Plus by the time you reach that area you're fatigued! I saw a lot of people stop around this area for a breather / rest. The view at mini world's end, world's end and the waterfall was nice and worth the effort!

The price is realy much too expensive (3000LKR/Person)!! The view is beautiful, but only at the parking area we saw some animals! No booklet, no brochure. The nature is awesome. the walk to little & greater world's end and bakers waterfall and back to the enttance is beautiful. offers you a diversity of nature and landscape. and there is no trash at the whole park.

Walked the standard Horton Plains 9km circular route and enjoyed every minute. We were surprised by the varied scenary and habitat. There is much to see in addition to the  dramatic views from Worlds End: birds and butterflies, rivers, waterfalls and mountains. We took 4 hours and could have spent a little more time. It is rocky underfoot in places so wear walking shoes

This was the best place to be hands down! Started early in the morning for the Sunrise, beautiful, mesmerizing views on the way, very cold in the morning but gets hot as the sun overheads. Haven't seen more beautiful views before, this 3 hours of trekking n hiking was the best experience ever! Flat rate for foreigners, a lil expensive but worth the views! Start from the left and you will see Mini worlds end first then worlds end and then Bakers Fall. My view to start from left as the waterfall in the end is like an oasis in the dessert.

We depart hotel at 5am in the morning for the hiking in Horton Plain. On the way to the entrance to the Horton Plain National Park, we met with wild moose who came closer to our van trying to get some food. Very very cute! At the entrance to the Hortain Plain, the staff check all the bags and make sure no plastic items were brought in the national park. Very good sense of protecting the mother nature that we should all learn from them! The 9KM hiking path is not paved roads and with ups and downs and I think it will be difficult in a bad weather. Our party (incl. two kids of 10 yrs old and my parents 73 and 74 yrs old) completed the circle in 3 hours and 20 minutes. But scenery is quite amazing and we all enjoyed the walk. When we completed the hiking and drived on to the next stop, we did not see any wild animals. Maybe that is also one of the reasons to get up early to start the hiking on the Horton Plain.

Somebody who was in Nuwara Eliya but haven't seen Horton plains missed the best part of his stay. Is a must for everybody. It doesn't matter if is cloudy or rainy. You don't need to be very sportive to get there around. Is nature pure.

We have traveled may parts of the world. I was a bit reluctant to get up at 5 to be there at 6, but what a dream! We were first at the World's end which made it extra special. What a spectacular view, another little piece of heaven. About 30 min later the fog came in, as it seems to do most days. We liked the hike through this beautiful park very much!

Visit Horton Plains early in the morning, i'd say no later than 7.00am.  Later it gets hot and busy and the mists can obliterate the views.  Take the circular route to the right and start in the direction of Baker's Falls and then loop around to World's End.  This way around means you have less steep inclines.  Its around 7 to 9 km in total but worth it.

It's very very amazing to visit the worlds end, it's so beautiful in there, the hike is wonderful but the walking way is not very good but still I like it, they protect the environment, it's better not to take any plastic items, chewing gums, and non decay able items.  The worlds end and mini worlds end view is awesome and the bakers falls is a highlight which we may not like to come out of. A very lovely place I've been.

The walk is not without its challenges (not least because our legs still hurt from Adam's Peak the day before), but it's satisfying. Get there early as the mist settles in and then there is no view at all. As far as World's End is concerned, it is impressive, but it lacks the sense of grandeur we were expecting. From Mini World's End take the unmarked path up and get a view of people standing at true World's End as this gives a great perspective. The falls are worth the trip and we found them to be very hypnotic to watch. The walk after the falls has some challenging moments and can feel quite long, especially when the mist settles in.

Visited here in February. Had to wait an hour and a half for our guide to get entrance tickets because the place was in complete chaos; no system for parking or dealing with the queue. This is a great visit and a comfortable scramble over reasonable ground that lasts about 2 1/2 hours with two amazing viewpoints at Worlds end and Little Worlds End. The high plateau area is teeming with wildlife and despite being a popular spot it is possible to find yourself alone on one of the meandering paths with a stunning view of the streams, waterfalls or local wildlife to keep you company. The view from World's end on a clear day is spectacular...860m straight down. Top tip: majority of visitors go clockwise round the park ie straight to the worlds end viewpoint. Try going anti-clockwise to avoid the crowds.

it is an easy walk manageble for everyone. They said it takes 4 hours but it only took us 2,5 hours. not much wildlife but beautiful nature. a bit busier at the actual worlds end. Be careful, there are no fences and we were told people have fallen down before. Dont forget your sunscreen and hat!

this is a place to go when you are physically well, and have a thirst for adventure. the distance to the world's end is looooooooooong! we didn't have any guide, we got lost and it started raining heavily, there is no shade to keep away from the rain so we were soaked and lost! Nuawara Eliya is very cold so I went home with a cold. However the views are amazing and breathtaking, its worth the walk I must add. very pricey!

There were three sights to see, little worlds end, great worlds end and bakers fall. So beautiful to see. I made the mistake of wearing flipflops! Patches are very rocky and muddy. Its best to go in the morning before the mist covers the view.

It's quite popular among Sri Lankans and Europeans as well. It's situated in Nuwara Eliya district and you need to have the transportation to access this place. Rules are strict and should be obeyed if you want to access this place. During Autumn period temperature increase up to avg. 20. During winter time, it drops to avg. 13.

World's end location is within the Horton Plains national park.  We took the circular trail which took us to 'World's End' and other attractions.  For a nature lover, the trail itself is a valuable experience.  From the point called World's End one can see the plains below and the breathtaking view of the mountains.  In the morning, it is spectacular.  Also depending on the time, you will see everything clearly and then suddenly you will see clouds emerging from the plains and covering everything, which gives the appearance that the end of the earth is at the location (hence called World's End).  Just a word of caution do not attempt to take selfies at the edge of the cliffs,  too dangerous and a fall to down below can be fatal.

We just took our time walking around the circular route and it wasn't too difficult. There were a few 'lumpy' places but generally the route was good with boots or stout walking shoes. The view from World's End was amazing and well worth the trek. I personally found the national park information boards, that are dotted along the route, very useful.

We had a great time hiking this almost 9k track. Nature is amazing and the views from the World's End are sweeping. Baker's fall is ok but there are better ones all over Sri Lanka. Wild life is all around, but we saw only one dear and of course many birds. You should start hiking at about 6 am, since almost every day after 10 o clock the place is totally covered with clouds and fog. It's a great place to hike, though you have to tolerate the hundreds of people that are doing the same (and most of them totally un equipped).

Our driver guided us on a roundabout trek to get to the top of the mountain.  It was really nice as it was less populated and we were able to see more of the countryside.  The views from the top are beautiful and can't be missed if you're in the area.

Horton Plains was fantastic! We got a car from our hotel (which they set up for us) - it arrived at 5am and we got to Horton plains by 6am where we joined the small queue for tickets. Tickets cost 3,000 rupees per person. The walk was absolutely brilliant, so beautiful and refreshing. Whilst there are lots of people doing the walk,  it didn't feel busy at all. Make sure you take layers with you as it is cold at times but when the sun comes out, it does get hot. Make sure you get up early as the mist comes at about 9am and this will obscure the view.

The whole hike was not only about World's End. It's beautiful, alright, but whole Horton Plains are. Just look around when you walk. Unfortunately, the guide books are right - you have to be there early to have views and avoid clouds. Departed from Nuwara Eliya at 5am, started hiking around 6:30am and by the time we were back, the clouds were already low and it was beginning to rain.

Of course this a must see sight, but I am not sure if it is as amazing as other reviews make you belief. Yes the World's End is a stunning view but it wasn't mind blowing. The walk is certainly nice, but it's not so special. The Baker's Falls are also nice but again, I have seen better... (Yes I am spoiled, I know). Before you commence the trail your bags are searched and potential litter. When your on the walk you unfortunately still find bottles, plastic, paper and other stuff, unbelievable! When you make the walk, do go for the full round and once you get the junction, pick the track on the right (so you come back on the one on the left). This one is more quiet since most people go left and many of them take the same route back. As mentioned, it's certainly a nice place to visit, but set your expectations to average.

Please do go for the trek. It is a 9km trek, not-so-difficult trek. Start very early on, by say 7am as the day is the clearest around 9-10 am, so the views from the world's end are the best. Use the loo right in the beginning of the park as they are better than the one which comes later into the trail. Also, you will experience different kinds of terrain - tropical rain forest narrow pathways, rocky tiny paths, muddy/slushy paths etc. Apply sunscreen or carry caps/shades. Have a great time there! :)

It's a nice nature walk but please carry a lot of water and refreshments! We left our hotel at 5.30am for World’s End.  The journey in pitch black darkness was worth it in its own right. The spooky silhouettes of trees rising starkly from the mists hovering above the fields made for some dramatic photo opps.  Sunrise was at 6 am and we spied sambar deer in the fields and also saw Adam’s Peak from afar. There is also a small scenic lake on route with mist floating above it.  About three quarters of the way up to the 2000 metres/6,600 feet high Horton Plains, was a vista point where we hopped out of our van to take several shots of the early morning light falling on the mountainside.  Be warned! At that altitude and time, it is very cold – it felt like 45F/7C – so bring a warm jacket. A shawl, two T-shirts and thin cotton top (what I pathetically had on) will not cut it. Most of the people I saw had on down or fleece jackets! Aside from warm clothes, the next most important thing to know is where the toilets are located. There are toilets at the ticket booth.  At this ungodly time, the toilets are still clean as not many people have used them, but please come with your own tissue as there is none provided.  Your driver will continue on for 1 km or so to the car park where he will be parked and waiting for your return. Here, there are some surprisingly clean squat toilets behind the canteen.  About 100 metres is the new Visitor Centre where there are toilet facilities.  About 1-1.5 km into the hike are toilets but when I checked them out, they were quite off-putting, not to mention they had no doors.  So unless you were terribly desperate and had an umbrella to provide makeshift privacy, this last toilet option is to be avoided. Many visitors at this hour would have had their hotel pack their breakfast. However, because of the fear of irresponsible visitors leaving their food debris in the park (bad for the park animals, not to mention that plastic can kill animals when swallowed), food in Styrofoam or other plastic containers is not allowed in; supermarket bottled water must have the plastic film wrapped around the bottle removed. The hike is along a river bed so there is little climbing. However, there are large rocks (where the rapids would be if the river was full) that require some negotiating and a walking stick is in order if you are not as sturdy as you would like. It is quite important to start this hike early otherwise rising mists would obscure the views at World’s End. I was there at 9 am and had half an hour of good views.  By 9.30 am mists were forming and I could not see the bottom half of the valley.  Another good reason to start early is that after Baker’s Falls, your route back to the car park would be pretty much in the open grasslands, and it already gets pretty hot between 10 am and 11 am.  Bring a hat and sunblock! In summary, leave your hotel at 5.30am latest, wear warm clothing, bring food in environmentally friendly packaging, bring a walking stick if necessary, a hat and sunblock, and toilet tissue.

Heaven on Earth, Above is my simple statement. I have been here many times and has spent days on the ground. This a precious piece of land on Sri Lanka, situated in the center of the country in the high lands. The climate and geography is termed as cloud forest. Due to high altitude and location, clouds sweep through the forest and created 365 days of drizzle or rain. The land is full of free running Sambar and if you are really lucky you will see a leopard (this is a very rare situation). You need to go there early in the morning for the best experience or stay till evening. If there is bit of mist and small drizzle, you wil find the place to be most exciting. There is a place called Worlds End, where there is a sheer drop from a cliff where the view is breathtaking. Please apply sun cream as the UV is high, also drink enough water before you leave. Plastic bottles and polythene is prohibited and confiscated by authorities at site.

The cooler temperatures here were a welcome break from the heat throughout the rest of the country. Our group tour size was reduced to half since the others thought it might be too challenging. Our walk leader set a reasonable pace that was not difficult at all. Even one person in our group who brought hiking poles to help with problem ankles had no issue keeping up. As long as you dress in layers in appropriate clothing with rain gear you will be fine. I saw many people without hats, rain jacket, flimsy shoes, one guy wearing the shower cap from his hotel to stay dry, one girl in a short filmy dress walking barefoot(!) and holding her dressy shoes and wondering how far they would get. When you arrive, literally, you are staring down into a huge valley. Sometimes you see the valley floor, sometimes it is obscured by clouds. But where you stand at World's End, you see the moisture rushing up the valley walls into the cloud forest, where it seemingly vanishes into the bright, blue skies over Horton Plains National Park. Relatively easy 8km round trip hike to get here. But it can be hot.

At first, I did not want to pay the high price to get into Horton's Plains. But I am SO glad I did. The 9.5 km hike takes about 4 hours, and is totally worth the money. As soon as you enter the park, you are met by beautiful views and a mysterious silence. Throughout your hike, you will get to see Mini World's End, World's End, and Bakers Falls. World's End was breathtaking- make sure you bring a camera! Also, make sure you begin your hike by 7:00 AM to avoid the fog that could obscure your view later in the day. And wear warm clothes- it is quite chilly in the morning!

An alarm call at 3.45 was not a good start but our guide knew exactly what he was doing. A 10  minute stop to watch the dawn and an arrival just 2 minutes before the gate opened. After a packed breakfast we set off at 7.00am completing the round trip in a leisurely 4 hours. The walk down the valley to Bakers falls was easy, although the long and steady uphill walk to Worlds End was tiring. The weather warmed up as the sun rose so fleeces came off and hats went on. However, the view from Worlds End was well worth all the effort as the weather was perfect and the view incredible. The walk away from Worlds End, up what appeared to be a dried river bed/waterfall was the low point. But at least walking this way round meant that we were in the shade of the forest during the heat of the late morning. While walking we saw Bear Monkeys, Sambar deer, Mountain Hawk Eagles, a Kestrel, several smaller endemic bird species quite happy to perch on the nearest foliage and a couple of lizards. The early start meant that these were visible as they vanish as the day progresses. At times I had found myself trailing a long way behind everyone else, wheezing like a steam train and was not always confident I could walk out - but the views are amazing and you just keep going and eventually you find you have walked all the way round. Did I enjoy it  - yes Would I do it again - mmm Did I know I had acute bronchitis - not until a day or so later when I called the doctor out.

I've been to World's End in February 2014, and it was a very pleasant experience traveling to the Horton's Plains. Horton Plains supposed to experience lots of rainfall during most part of the year, but we were lucky to visit the place on a perfect sunny day with a temperature of not more than 25 Celsius. That's the perfect smooth weather to visit Nuwara Eliya and surroundings! There are two routes to World's End, once you reach to the Wild Life department check point in Horton's Plains. Take the longer route (5 KM walk), and comeback on the shorter route (3KM walk). If you are ready to walk for 8 KM on Horton's Planins, you are assured to get one of the best hiking experiences you can have in any parts of the world. Wild Life department of Sri Lanka has done a marvelous job to preserve this world heritage sight. Few years back, Horton's Plains was threatened by pollution caused by tourism activities, but now the department is taking tough measures to control unhealthy tourist activities. Good job!

We left our hotel before dawn to head up to the escarpment to see Horton's Plain and Worlds End. We weren't sure what to expect, but we were told it was a must-see whilst in the hill country, so we were expecting great things. It was quite a trek by 4X4 to get up there, and it was light when we arrived to set off on foot along the trail to worlds end.  The trail started off very easy across scrubland with a nice wide and fairly even path, but after a mile or 2 it got more and more rutted and was quite hard work, even for us as relatively fit people.  We passed Little Worlds End first, and even that was an impressive drop as you peered over the edge.  However World's end was a real drop of over a kilometre!  There are no safety fences here, and our guide told us that two Aussie girls had fallen over the month before (one tried to grab the other to stop her falling, and they both ended up going over).  Being so high, and with the haze below it was difficult to make out much of a view, but it certainly was a huge distance to the valley below.  The walk back to where we'd left the 4X4 took us back past Bakers Falls, which unfortunately was not very impressive as the rains hadn't come this year, but we could see that it would be a good sight if we'd come after the rains on a normal year. We'd hoped to see plenty of wildlife up there, but other than a few birds, the wildlife was pretty sparse. There was a rather run-down visitor centre/museum at the end of the walk which had a few interesting exhibits and told us what wildlife was there before the colonial British shot it all years ago. All in all, a fairly interesting day, but we were not as enamored as we'd hoped!

If you are going to Sri Lanka on a holiday then visiting the Horton Plains should definitely be on your itinerary. It is an 8.5 kms world heritage looping nature trail where you can be excused of imagining that you are the only inhabitants of this vast world until you happen to pass by a few groups of travellers like you. You reach this place from Nuwara Eliya which in itself is a charming holiday destination up in the hills. You would pass by a number of huge tea estates and you can enter one (no entrance fee) to take a short conducted tour of the factory and stop by factory shop to taste the tea produced there and buy some to take home if you wish. Coming back to the Horton Plains, the highlights of this trek are the Baker falls, mini world's end and world's end. The roaring falls with the water spray hitting you make for a refreshing scenery. The world's end as the name suggests certainly appears to be the end point of the world. The amazing place has a 'cloud forest'' where you can literally see the clouds forming and rolling in to hit you gently. The mist enveloping the valley below makes it appear that there is nothing but vastness of space beyond the point where you stand. A word of caution - be alert and cautious, especially when you are travelling with kids as there may be a temptation to go the very edge of the plateau to experience the thrill.

World's End wasn't quite what I expected from the descriptions but the view is still pretty nice, just not all that different from other high points in the tea country. The walk was quite nice, not very challenging although fairly long. The scenery was really quite unlike anything else in Sri Lanka, it reminded me more of the button grass plains of Tasmania!

You are walking 8 miles with a lot of people quickly in a rocky riverbed to get to a view, while nice, isn't any better than any other stupendous view you see everywhere you go in the tea country. The elderly and children might find it quite difficult, in fact while we were hiking a tourist had a heart attack and died upon completion. The walk up to the world's end can be long and tiring yet interesting. You would also get to see the Baker's Falls on your way there and this would be quiet worth the effort. The long 9km trek is one that requires a good level of fitness AND good walking shoes. The paths are rocky, uneven and require lots of scrambling up or down steep slopes over tree roots and so forth. Fortunately it was dry for our trip but I can imagine it being very slippery. We chose not to go down to Bakers falls as the way down was badly eroded and slippery and we did not want to risk injury. We were not alone in making this decision. This is a place that you definitely have to get up early to see. The admission fees are a little confusing - listed in US$ but only Rupee accepted. Also there were ++ to fees (service fee VAT and charges for car and driver) It is a good idea to layer up in clothes so you can peel off as the day warms up. NOTE Don't forget to take your own toilet paper as none is provided but the 2 basic toilets were kept clean. If you are carrying bottled water, attendants at the gate remove the plastic security wrap as well as the labels. I assume that it is to prevent litter. We saw one deer, one native bird (Sri Lankas national symbol) and only heard the monkeys in the distance, so don't be too disappointed if you don't see any animals.

We stayed the night before at the bungalow inside the park so it was easy for us to start the hike real early. You need to get there early before 9:00 am since the fog rolls in around that time and you don't see anything. We were able to experience the clear views before the fog.

We went there in pouring rain and clouds, but when we came up at the national park the clouds dissappeard. Really nice and a somewhat odd landscape. We saw some of World's end between the clouds and a big waterfall. Also saw some sambar deer and lot of birds (endemic!). Make sure you take the path the right way so you have to climb less at the end (first the waterfall, than worlds end and little worlds end).

You are just mesmerized by the sight of this place. A cloud forest that too reachable by just walking and no climbing. Just sitting there and feeling clouds on your face is an amazing experience. A must must go and pray that you land there in conducive weather.

I have probably visited this place more than 20 times and this is one of the places I love in this country. When you reach here you may wonder whether you are actually in Sri Lanka or somewhere else. You could book bungalows through Wild Life Conservation Department and your visit is not complete if you do not stay up in Hortan Plains. The weather changes so quickly you would wonder from where that comes down and suddenly disappears. If you are lucky enough then you may see a leopard and there are other types of animals as well. Place is well known for some of the rare birds and beautiful flowers.

I went here some ....14 years ago now (the drop-down won't let me put in the right date) and it was something I still remember vividly, We rose early for the 4x4 journey to near the top, then began our walk. Allow a good 45 mins extra in a van, to get to the starting point of the walk, as the road's not great getting there. Look out for Sambar deer on the way up in the fields. It was very wet when we got there, and our guide was advised to only take us to Little World's End.  There had been a lot of rain which made climbing up then down a waterfall a bit too dangerous, so we were happy to take the easier route. The route we took was perfect for our level of walking - we also didn't have the most appropriate footwear.  When we got to the viewing point it was impressive, however the cloud cover comes in fast as you're so high.  Don't forget the camera! But stay away from the edge, it's a sheer drop and there's absolutely no fence to stop you falling down.

Is World's End nice? Yes. Is it awe-inspiring? No. Is it worth trekking 9km. Heck No!  You can get nicer views from the roadside. And I thought the waterfalls at Bambarakanda (in Badulla) and Diyaluma were much nicer than the Bakers Fall (which was up and down a very, very steep ravine.  Much of the hike is not even visually beautiful, so you're just trekking to get to the mini world's end and World's End. Underwhelming! The highlight is the beautiful savannah at the return end (which is also mostly level ground). I further disagree with all the reviewers who say that you should get up and out at some ungodly hour to get the best views.  I actually think there was nothing particularly beautiful about the break of dawn view, and think that the mountains peeking through the clouds is more beautiful than either the mini or full-on World's End.  Sri Lanka is a beautiful country, but don't make the mistake of letting the guide book tell you what's the most beautiful place in the country.  Unless you just like walking, you should pull over on the side of the road on your way through the mountains and get your fill of the beautiful scenery.

World's End in Horton Plains National Park is not the most spectacular hike in the world, but, we really enjoyed ourselves. Be absolutely sure you bring a breakfast and do make sure you arrive early or you will not get good views. We hired a guide as we were interested in the flora. Our guide was very knowledgeable and allowed us to go at ou own speed allowing lots of time for photography. The views from worlds end were beautiful, although being from Canada' Rocky Mountains, we have seen more spectacular for free.

Wonderful views throughout the 9k hike, not just the two World's End locations and Baker's Falls.  Not a technical hike either and suitable for most.  Only complaint, like so many others, is the cost - private driver to get there + high fees to get in.  And don't bother reading the rate schedule that is posted as they will be charging you what they please.

Well for starters we left our hotel at around 6:00 am. Ensure you carry packed breakfast. Overall it was a nice trek for about 3 hours which culminated with the breath taking Bakers fall, which was the saving grace. Will I return again. Yes definitely.

We live in hiking country so to be fair are not that easily impressed.  But by developing country standards I would say that this is a well developed, well marked and well managed park. It was quiet, we were there around 09:00 so later than european tourists and earlier than Sri lankan tourists. It's a lovely walk with nice views and made for a good morning out.  The scenery on the way up is just as interesting as the park, in a way, but then it was our first turpentine forest. We started out from Ella at 5am. The road up to the Park Entrance from Haputale was very scenic. The guards at the entrance to the walk insist that you remove all plastic - the seals on the top of water bottles for example. The view at Worlds End exceeded our expectations, and one fascinating thing was seeking how quickly the clouds rolled in after we had eaten our breakfast. My advice is that you can't start early enough on this walk. Take your time and you will miss one of the highlights of a trip to Sri Lanka.  What we found unexpected was the poor eroded state of the track. Often it was little better than a stream bed. So you do need good waterproof shoes.

When left our hotel at 6am and we beat the holidaying Sri Lankans.  We had good hiking shoes and were amazed to see locals in very loose footwear. This place is beautiful but a small investment in getting paths better where the is delicate ecology or where the footing is suspect would make this place world class.

There are no words to describe the beauty of this location. World's End is a must visit when staying in Nuwara Eliya. The entire walk is about a 9Km circular track which takes about 3-4 hours to complete, and takes you through varying scenery across Horton's plains to more uphill treks to view Baker's Falls. But the definite highlight of the walk is mini World's End and World's End which is about 3 times higher. Make sure you start out early and so to reach World's End before 10am to see the Forest of Clouds. We were very fortunate as we made it around 9:30am just in time to see the mists rise which is unforgettable. Carry plenty of water and sunscreen but overall a must do! The only downfall was that we didn't see much wildlife but would do it again.

This is excellent 2-3 hors walk through beautiful nature. Hills, river , waterfalls - all this creates idyllic scenario. World's end gives you nice view (if there is no fog or clouds) but for us it wasn't main  attraction of the walk. Worth to see

I understand Sri Lanka is a poor country but beautiful countryside in the uk is free to explore. entry fee is fine, but make it  reasonable....

Go early and avoid the crowds (it was a public holiday when we went and it all got a bit manic).  The roads are quite precarious and the locals drive like demons.  A guided walk through Horton Plains is a really great way to spend a morning.

Must visit place, BUT you must find the time on your visit because the journey up and down from Nuwara Eliya to Horton Plains takes about 2 hours up & down and another 3 hours at least on trek. BUT it is well worth your while. Situated at an elevation of over 7500 Feet it is bio diversity at its greatest. You do all the climbing on your journey by car. Once you get to Horton Plains you are on a plateau on the Hill top and your trek is on near flat ground, the trees are dwarfed due to the intense cold, you see elk in the distance, the origins of some of the principal rivers of Sri Lanka. The trek should be taken at leisure, savouring all the beauties of nature around as you approach the Worlds End, where, on a clear day you could see Beragala Pass in Haputale, and then take the "short cut"(  which is slightly longer" passing Bakers Falls and return. It is a trek well worth the experience. I do not agree with the step like path way that has been constructed with cement as the step  height does not synchronize with convenient weary free walking pace.

We were made to use a 'jeep' to get there, but I don't think that is necessary.  The road is paved, and the 'jeep' is a van which was in terrible condidition.  For $40, I expected more, but I would rather have the option not to pay it. We were also given a guide, but this was not necessary either as for most of the way the trail is well marked, certainly to both "end of the world's".  The views from these spots is spectacular, then you can really realize that you are in fact on a high plain. The trail continues to Baker Falls, a lovely waterfall hidden in the forest part of the park.  The trail is less well marked here, and the guide was helpful here to get over fallen trees and rather large rocks which are the make up of the trail. The climb out of the falls is easier, and you can take a few minutes to watch the falls from some bleachers which have been setup. The walk from the falls to the entrance is very nice and relaxing. Wear sunscreen, I was decieved as the morning had the park covered in fog which quickly burned off, and the cooler tempurature was deceiving.

Was a little cloudy when we went so we weren't too blown away with the view - we prefered mini world's end but there was lots of wildlife to see on route and we enjoyed Baker's falls. It gets hot so wear sunscreen and get there early.

We are both over 70 and found the flat easy, but a lot of it was up and down the dried up creek beds which were full of large rocks that you had to get up and down.   We took our time and were happy to have achieved this trek - their are 2 important views - 1 called little worlds end and the final one was IT!   Great views but a bit hazy - you could see forever.   Around 10/12 kilometers from start to finish.

Ask to be driven to the Horton plains visitor center (ca. 1,5 h on windy roads with wonderful views). You should set off from Nuwara Eliya at about 05:30 just before sunrise to be at the visitor center at about 07:00. At the visitor center in the middle of nowhere you find a big carpark with minivans, busses etc. All sorts of groups arrive with drivers and guides. You have to pay an entrance fee. Be under the first ones and most of all walk straight to the big worlds end which you will reach at about 08:30-09:00: Then you have a chance of the spectacular far view from the plateau over a steep and about 900m high cliff. As the sun rises quickly and it becomes warm clouds will form and at about 09:30 to 10:00 (when we arrived) you will face the pure imagination of it – a dense white nothing. The 9km / 3 h walk on uneven eroded paths that like firm shoes is beautiful and reminds a bit of a tropical version of Scotland. Fog arises from the trees, you can see deer and some nice birds – again: try to be on your own and enjoy it quietly. Another advantage if you start early: You are back in the car park at 12:00 - to 12:30 walking relaxed, taking pics and having a sit down at worlds end and the baker falls. So you are back in NE at about 14:00 and could perfectly visit a tea estate...

Horton plains is very pleasant. The view from worlds end was nice but not spectacular. That said, it was quite hazy when I visted so perhaps it is normally better. Try and get a wildlife guide to walk with you and point out animals - they are hard to see if you are by yourself.

As there was fog coming on and off, the view from Mini World's End was more spectacular than from World's End itself (to me, the view was more spectacular even than from the Adam's Peak). It's a nice landscape - again something different to other landscapes in the southwest - and there are times when you don't hear any other sounds than the humming of bees or bellowing of monkeys. Bakers falls are not that interesting, but the round course makes for a good walk - good shoes and water/food supply are recommended.

World's End is located within the Horton Plains National Park. The visitors are warned that you will end up paying around 1700 Sri Lankan Rupees per person as an entry fee apart from other charges. Locals have to pay only Rs. 60. There is a nature trail which takes about 3 hours at normal walking speed to cover on foot. once you start the trail then its just one way. its quite scenic, rocky, adventurous and interesting.
